id_tips: Male is crested and entirely red with a black mask around a thick orange-red bill. Female is warm tan with a red crest, wings, and tail, and the same thick bill. Both sexes raise the crest when alert.
habitat: Yards, thickets, forest edges, and suburban shrubs year-round.
wnc: One of the most familiar birds in every part of North Carolina, including mountain towns.
uses: Song is a loud whistled cheer-cheer-cheer or birdy-birdy-birdy, and the call is a sharp chip. Eats seeds, fruit, and insects. A regular feeder bird.
caution: Native songbirds are protected. Enjoy them at feeders and leave nests alone.
lookalikes: Summer Tanager males are red but have no crest and no black mask, and the bill is paler. Scarlet Tanager males have black wings.

The northern cardinal (Cardinalis cardinalis), also commonly known as the common cardinal, red cardinal, or simply cardinal, is a bird in the genus Cardinalis. It can be found in southeastern Canada, through the eastern United States from Maine to Minnesota to Texas, New Mexico, southern Arizona, southern California and south through Mexico, Belize, and Guatemala. It is also an introduced species in a few locations such as Bermuda and all major islands of Hawaii since its introduction in 1929. Its habitat includes woodlands, gardens, shrublands, and wetlands. It is the state bird of Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, North Carolina, Ohio, Virginia, and West Virginia.

id_tips: Small, rusty-brown, with a bold white eyebrow and a long, slightly curved bill. The tail is often cocked. Larger and warmer-colored than a House Wren.
habitat: Brush piles, porches, garages, tangles, and wooded yards. Nests in odd cavities.
wnc: A year-round voice in the mountains, piedmont, and coastal plain. Hard winters can knock numbers down.
uses: Song is a loud, rolling tea-kettle, tea-kettle, tea-kettle. Eats insects and spiders and will come to suet.
caution: Native and protected. Nest boxes and porch corners are normal nest sites. Leave the nest until the young leave.
lookalikes: House Wren is smaller, grayer, and lacks the strong white eyebrow. Bewick's Wren is rare in North Carolina and has white in the tail corners.

The Carolina wren (Thryothorus ludovicianus) is a species of wren common in the eastern United States, the extreme south of Ontario, Canada, the northeast and southeast of Mexico, and into northern Central America. Severe winters restrict the northern limits of their range, while favorable weather conditions lead to a northward extension of their breeding range. Their preferred habitat is in dense cover in forest, farm edges, and suburban areas. This wren is the state bird of South Carolina.
Ten subspecies are recognized, occurring across the range of the species; they differ slightly in song and appearance. It is generally inconspicuous, avoiding the open for extended periods of time. When out in the open, they energetically investigate their surroundings and are rarely stationary. After finding a mate, pairs maintain a territory and stay together for several years. id_tips: Gray above, pale below, with a pointed crest, a black forehead patch, and peach wash on the flanks. Large dark eye.
habitat: Deciduous woods, yards, and feeders. Often travels with chickadees.
wnc: Common year-round across the state, including mountain coves and towns.
uses: Song is a clear whistled peter-peter-peter. Eats insects, seeds, and acorns, and carries sunflower seeds away to hammer them open.
caution: Native and protected. A feeder regular, not a pest.
lookalikes: Chickadees are smaller, have a black cap and bib, and no crest. A waxwing has a crest but is sleek, masked, and yellow-tipped at the tail.
wikipedia_extract: The tufted titmouse (Baeolophus bicolor) is a small songbird native to eastern North America. The species belongs to the tit and chickadee family (Paridae). The black-crested titmouse, found from central and southern Texas southward, was originally included as a subspecies but now is considered a separate species, Baeolophus atricristatus.

id_tips: Tiny, with a black cap and bib, white cheeks, and gray wings with pale edging. The lower edge of the black bib looks neater than a Black-capped Chickadee's.
habitat: Woods, yards, and feeders. Nests in cavities and nest boxes.
wnc: The chickadee of North Carolina. Black-capped Chickadees occur only along the far northern edge of the high mountains, if at all.
uses: Call is a fast chickadee-dee-dee, higher and faster than a Black-capped. Song is a clear four-note fee-bee fee-bay. Eats insects and seeds.
caution: Native and protected. They use small nest boxes. Leave active nests in place.
lookalikes: Black-capped Chickadee has more white in the wing and a slower, hoarser call. In most of North Carolina a chickadee is this species.
wikipedia_extract: The Carolina chickadee (Poecile carolinensis) is a small, non-migratory passerine bird in the tit family Paridae. It has a black cap and bib, and distinctive white cheeks. The bird looks extremely similar to the black-capped chickadee. It is largely found in the southeastern and central United States.

id_tips: Dark gray above, brick-orange breast, yellow bill, and a broken white eye-ring. Often runs on lawns and stops to pull earthworms.
habitat: Lawns, parks, orchards, and open woods. Large winter flocks use fruiting trees.
wnc: Present statewide. Many leave the high mountains in winter, then flocks return with spring.
uses: Song is a cheerful, rising and falling cheerily-cheer-up. Eats earthworms, insects, and fruit.
caution: Native and protected. Lawn chemicals reduce the insects and worms they hunt.
lookalikes: Eastern Towhee has orange sides but a black or brown hood, white belly, and red eye, and it scratches in leaves rather than running on open lawns.

The American robin (Turdus migratorius) is a migratory bird of the true thrush genus and Turdidae, the wider thrush family. It is named after the European robin because of its reddish-orange breast, though the two species are not closely related, with the European robin belonging to the Old World flycatcher family. The American robin is widely distributed throughout North America, wintering from southern Canada to central Mexico and along the Pacific coast.
According to the Partners in Flight database (2019), the American robin is the most abundant landbird in North America (with 370 million individuals), ahead of red-winged blackbirds, introduced European starlings, mourning doves and house finches. It has seven subspecies.

id_tips: Crested, bright blue above, white below, with a black necklace and white spots in the wings and tail. Noisy and bold at feeders.
habitat: Oak woods, yards, and parks.
wnc: Common year-round across the state. Fall migrants can pass through in big groups.
uses: Calls include a harsh jay-jay and a squeaky pump-handle note. Eats acorns, seeds, insects, and sometimes eggs. Buries acorns and helps plant oaks.
caution: Native and protected. They can empty a feeder. That is not a reason to harm them.
lookalikes: Nothing else in North Carolina is this large, blue, and crested. Eastern Bluebirds are smaller, have rusty breasts, and no crest.
wikipedia_extract:
The blue jay (Cyanocitta cristata) is a passerine bird in the family Corvidae, native to eastern North America. It lives in most of the eastern and central United States; some eastern populations may be migratory. Resident populations are also in Newfoundland, Canada; breeding populations are found across southern Canada. It breeds in both deciduous and coniferous forests, and is common in residential areas. Its coloration is predominantly blue, with a white chest and underparts, and a blue crest; it has a black, U-shaped collar around its neck and a black border behind the crest. Males and females are similar in size and plumage, which does not vary throughout the year. Four subspecies have been recognized.

id_tips: Slender and gray, with white patches in the wings that flash in flight and white outer tail feathers. Often sings from a wire or rooftop.
habitat: Lawns, farms, towns, and shrubby edges.
wnc: Common in towns and valleys statewide. A bit scarcer in the highest, most forested coves.
uses: Song copies other birds, one phrase repeated several times before switching. Eats insects and fruit, and defends berry bushes.
caution: Native and protected. A bird that dive-bombs you in spring is guarding a nest. Walk past and leave it.
lookalikes: Gray Catbird is slatier, has a black cap, and a chestnut patch under the tail, and it does not flash white wing patches. Brown Thrasher is rusty and streaked below.
wikipedia_extract:
The northern mockingbird (Mimus polyglottos) is a mockingbird commonly found in North America, of the family Mimidae. The species is also found in some parts of the Caribbean, as well as on the Hawaiian Islands. It is typically a permanent resident across much of its range, but northern mockingbirds may move farther south during inclement weather or prior to the onset of winter. The northern mockingbird has gray to brown upper feathers and a paler belly. Its tail and wings have white patches which are visible in flight.
The species is known for its ability to mimic bird calls and other types of sound, including artificial and electronic noises. Studies have shown its ability to identify individual humans and treat them differently based on learned threat assessments. It is an omnivore and consumes fruit, invertebrates, and small vertebrates. It is often found in open areas, open woodland

id_tips: Male is bright blue above with a rusty throat and breast and a white belly. Female is grayer with blue in the wings and tail and a paler rusty wash.
habitat: Open fields with scattered trees, orchards, golf courses, and nest boxes. Sits on wires and drops to the grass for insects.
wnc: Year-round across the state where the land is open. Nest boxes brought them back after cavity competition.
uses: Song is a soft, warbled chur-wi or tru-ly. Eats insects in summer and berries in winter.
caution: Native and protected. House Sparrows and European Starlings take over boxes. A bluebird box needs a 1.5-inch hole and monitoring.
lookalikes: Indigo Bunting is smaller and all blue, with no rusty breast. Blue Jay is much larger, crested, and patterned in black and white.
wikipedia_extract:
The eastern bluebird (Sialia sialis) is a small North American migratory thrush found in open woodlands, farmlands, and orchards.
The bright-blue breeding plumage of the male, easily observed on a wire or open perch, makes this species a favorite of birders. The male's call includes sometimes soft warbles of jeew or chir-wi, or the melodious song chiti WEEW wewidoo.
It is the state bird of Missouri and New York.

id_tips: Slim, warm tan, with a small head, black spots on the wing, and a long pointed tail with white edges. Wings whistle on takeoff.
habitat: Fields, wires, feeders, and gravel roads. Builds a flimsy stick nest.
wnc: Abundant statewide year-round, including mountain valleys.
uses: Song is a soft, mournful coo-OO, oo, oo, oo. Eats seeds. A legal game bird in season, and also a common yard bird.
caution: Hunting is regulated by season and license. Outside the season they are protected. Do not confuse them with the introduced collared-dove.
lookalikes: Eurasian Collared-Dove is chunkier and paler, with a black half-collar and a squared tail. Rock Pigeon is heavier and usually gray with a white rump.
wikipedia_extract:
The mourning dove (Zenaida macroura) is a member of the dove family, Columbidae. The bird is also known as the American mourning dove, the rain dove, and colloquially as the turtle dove, and it was once known as the Carolina pigeon and Carolina turtledove. It is one of the most abundant and widespread North American birds and a popular gamebird, with more than 20 million birds (up to 70 million in some years) shot annually in the U.S., both for sport and meat. Its ability to sustain its population under such pressure is due to its prolific breeding; in warm areas, one pair may raise up to six broods of two young each in a single year. The wings make an unusual whistling sound upon take-off and landing, a form of sonation. The bird is a strong flier, capable of speeds up to 88 km/h (55 mph).

id_tips: Male has red on the forehead, eyebrow, and breast, with brown streaking down the sides and a short, curved bill. Female is plain brown and heavily streaked, with no strong face pattern.
habitat: Towns, feeders, parking lots, and weedy edges.
wnc: Introduced to the eastern United States from the West and now common year-round across North Carolina, including mountain towns. It is not native to the East.
uses: Song is a lively warble that often ends in a harsh, buzzy note. Eats seeds, buds, and fruit. A dominant feeder finch.
caution: Introduced in the East. Can spread house-finch eye disease at crowded feeders. Clean feeders if you see swollen, crusty eyes.
lookalikes: Purple Finch, a native winter visitor, is more raspberry-red over the head and back, with less brown streaking on the sides. American Goldfinch has a smaller conical bill and, in summer, a black cap and wings.
wikipedia_extract: The house finch (Haemorhous mexicanus) is a North American bird in the finch family. It is native to Mexico and southwestern United States, but has since been introduced to the eastern part of North America and Hawaiʻi, and is found year-round in almost all parts of the United States and most of Mexico, with breeding grounds well into Canada as far north as northern Alberta. There are estimated to be 40 million house finches across North America, making it the second-most populous finch, just behind the American goldfinch. The house finch and the other two American rosefinches (Cassin's and purple finch) are placed in the genus Haemorhous.

id_tips: Stocky and short-tailed, with a long yellow bill in summer and a dark bill in winter. Plumage looks black at a distance but is glossy purple-green, and winter birds are spangled with pale spots. Walks on lawns instead of hopping.
habitat: Towns, farms, feedlots, and cavity trees. Huge winter roosts.
wnc: Invasive and established statewide after an 1890 introduction in New York. Competes with native cavity nesters.
uses: Song is a jumble of squeaks, whistles, and mimicked notes. Eats insects, grain, and fruit. Not protected by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act.
caution: Invasive. Takes nest holes from bluebirds, woodpeckers, and Purple Martins. Do not put up a martin house and then ignore starlings.
lookalikes: Common Grackle is larger and longer-tailed, with a pale eye. Blackbirds do not have the starling's yellow summer bill and spangled winter coat.

The common starling (Sturnus vulgaris), also known simply as the starling in Great Britain and Ireland, and as the European starling in North America, is a medium-sized passerine bird in the starling family, Sturnidae. It is about 20 cm (8 in) long and has glossy black plumage with a metallic sheen, which is speckled with white at some times of the year. The legs are pink and the bill is black in winter and yellow in summer; young birds have browner plumage than the adults. Its gift for mimicry has been noted in literature including the Mabinogion and the works of Pliny the Elder and William Shakespeare.

id_tips: Male has a gray crown, chestnut nape, black bib, and pale cheeks. Female is plain tan with a pale eyebrow and a thick seed-eater bill. Not in the native sparrow family.
habitat: Cities, barns, fast-food lots, and nest boxes. Rare in deep forest.
wnc: Invasive and established around people statewide. Less common in wild mountain forest than in towns.
uses: Calls are a monotonous cheep and a rattling chatter. Eats grain, crumbs, and seeds. Not protected by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act.
caution: Invasive. Kills nestlings and takes over bluebird and martin boxes. It is not a native sparrow that you should encourage.
lookalikes: Native sparrows are streakier or have cleaner face patterns and do not show the male's black bib and gray crown together. Eurasian Tree Sparrow is not established in North Carolina.

The house sparrow (Passer domesticus) is a bird of the sparrow family Passeridae, found in most parts of the world. It is a small bird that has a typical length of 16 cm (6.3 in) and a mass of 24–39.5 g (0.85–1.39 oz). Females and young birds are coloured pale brown and grey, and males have brighter black, white, and brown markings. One of 28 species in the genus Passer, the house sparrow is native to most of Europe, the Mediterranean Basin, and a large part of Asia. Its intentional or accidental introductions to many regions, including parts of Australasia, Africa, and the Americas, make it the most widely distributed wild bird.

id_tips: Chunky town pigeon. The wild-type bird is gray with two black wing bars, an iridescent neck, and a white rump. Feral birds can be white, black, red, or checkered.
habitat: Bridges, downtown buildings, barns, and grain elevators. Nests on ledges.
wnc: Introduced from Europe and established in cities and farms across the state, including mountain towns. Not a forest bird.
uses: Song is a low coo-coo-coo. Eats grain and spilled food. Not protected by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act.
caution: Introduced. Droppings under roosts are a building problem. Do not treat a Mourning Dove or a Collared-Dove as a pigeon.
lookalikes: Mourning Dove is slimmer, tan, and long-tailed. Eurasian Collared-Dove is pale tan with a thin black neck collar and no white rump.

The rock dove (Columba livia), also known as the common pigeon or rock pigeon (but see also Petrophassa), is a member of the bird family Columbidae (doves and pigeons). In common usage, it is often simply referred to as the "pigeon", although the rock dove is the wild form of the bird; the pigeons familiar to most people are the domesticated forms of the wild rock dove.
Wild rock doves are uniformly pale grey with two black bars on each wing, with few differences being seen between males and females; i.e. they are not strongly sexually dimorphic. The domestic pigeon, often called "Columba livia domestica", which includes about 1,000 different breeds, is descended from this species. Escaped domestic pigeons are the origin of feral pigeons around the world. Both forms can vary widely in the colour and pattern of their plumage unlike their wild ancestor, being red, brown, checkered, uniform

habitat: Suburbs, grain bins, and small-town wires.
wnc: Introduced and now a regular breeding bird in the piedmont and coastal plain. Still thinner in the high mountains, but spreading.
uses: Song is a three-note coo-COO-cook, often repeated. Eats grain and seeds. North Carolina treats it as a nonnative dove.
caution: Introduced. It is not protected as a native migratory bird. Do not shoot or harass native Mourning Doves by mistake.
lookalikes: Mourning Dove lacks the black collar and has a pointed tail. The rare African Collared-Dove is a cage bird and is not the established town dove.
wikipedia_extract: The Eurasian collared dove (Streptopelia decaocto), often called the collared dove, is a dove species from the genus Streptopelia. It is grey-buff to pinkish-grey, and has a black half-collar edged with white on its nape, alluding to the name. It is native to Europe, Asia, and North Africa. It has also been introduced to Japan, North and Central America, and select Caribbean islands.

id_tips: All black, including the bill and legs, with a fan-shaped tail in flight. Larger than a grackle and smaller than a raven. The call is the familiar caw.
habitat: Farms, roads, woods edges, and towns. Roosts in big winter flocks.
wnc: The common crow of the mountains and most of the state. Fish Crows are more coastal and piedmont and say a nasal uh-uh.
uses: Call is a clear caw. Eats almost anything: insects, waste grain, carrion, eggs, and fruit. Intelligent and social.
caution: Native and protected. They are not the introduced black birds. Starlings are smaller and short-tailed.
lookalikes: Fish Crow is best told by the nasal call. Common Raven is larger, with a wedge-shaped tail and a deep croak, and is a mountain and cliff bird. Grackles have long keel-shaped tails and pale eyes.

The American crow (Corvus brachyrhynchos) is a large passerine bird species of the family Corvidae. It is a common bird found throughout much of North America, only absent from the tundra biome. The American crow is the New World counterpart to the carrion crow and the hooded crow of Eurasia, occupying similar ecological niches.
The American crow has all-black plumage, with iridescent feathers. It looks similar to other all-black corvids. It is highly intelligent, similar to other Corvidae, and is adaptable to human environments. 
The American crow can be distinguished from the common raven by its smaller size and a slightly less pronounced beak, and from the carrion crow by its size, as the carrion crow is larger and of a stockier build. id_tips: Male is black on the hood, back, and tail, with rusty sides and a white belly. Female replaces the black with warm brown. Both have a red eye in the East and flash white tail corners. Scratches in leaf litter with both feet.
habitat: Brushy edges, clearcuts, and thickets.
wnc: A common breeding bird of shrubby places statewide, and many stay through winter in the lower mountains and piedmont.
uses: Song is drink-your-tea, the tea trilled. Call is a rising chewink or tow-hee. Eats seeds, fruit, and insects raked from the leaves.
caution: Native and protected. Brush piles and field edges are its habitat. Mowing every thicket removes it.
lookalikes: American Robin has an orange breast too, but it is plain gray above, has a yellow bill, and runs on lawns. Spotted Towhee is western and is not the Carolina bird.

The eastern towhee (Pipilo erythrophthalmus), also known as chewink, joree, or joree bird, is a large New World sparrow. The taxonomy of the towhees has been under debate in recent decades, and formerly this bird and the spotted towhee were considered a single species, the rufous-sided towhee.
Their breeding habitat is brushy areas across eastern North America. They nest either low in bushes or on the ground under shrubs. Northern birds migrate to the southern United States. One of this species was recorded as a vagrant to western Europe, a single bird in Great Britain in 1966.
The song is a short drink your teeeeea lasting around one second, starting with a sharp call ("drink!") and ending with a short trill "teeeeea". The name "towhee" is onomatopoeic description of one of the towhee's most common calls, a short, two-part call rising in pitch and sometimes also called a "chewink" call.

id_tips: Small and clean-breasted. Breeding birds have a bright rusty cap, a white eyebrow, and a black line through the eye. Winter birds are duller but still unstreaked below, with a gray rump.
habitat: Short grass, driveways, pines, and feeders.
wnc: A very common summer bird statewide and present in winter in much of the piedmont and coastal plain.
uses: Song is a dry, rapid trill on one pitch. Eats small seeds and insects. Often feeds on the ground under feeders.
caution: Native and protected. It is not a House Sparrow. The plain breast and rusty cap separate them.
lookalikes: Field Sparrow has a pink bill and a blanker face. House Sparrow males have a black bib and a gray crown. Song Sparrows are streaked below and pump the tail.

The chipping sparrow (Spizella passerina) is a species of New World sparrow, a passerine bird in the family Passerellidae. It is widespread, fairly tame, and common across most of its North American range.
The chipping sparrow has five subspecies. This bird is a partial migrant with northerly populations flying southwards in the fall to overwinter in Mexico and the southern United States, and flying northward again in spring.

id_tips: Brown and streaked, with a central breast spot where the streaks meet, a grayish eyebrow, and thick malar stripes. Pumps its long, rounded tail in flight.
habitat: Wet ditches, brush, marshes, and backyard edges.
wnc: Present year-round in much of the state. More widespread in winter, when northern birds join local ones.
uses: Song starts with a few clear notes and then a jumble of trills. Eats seeds and insects. Often sings from a low shrub.
caution: Native and protected. A streaked brown sparrow in a ditch is usually this bird, not an introduced sparrow.
lookalikes: House Sparrow is chunkier, with an unstreaked breast. Savannah Sparrow is usually in short grass and has a yellow lore. Fox Sparrow is larger and redder.
wikipedia_extract: The song sparrow (Melospiza melodia) is a medium-sized New World sparrow. Among the native sparrows in North America, it is easily one of the most abundant, variable, and adaptable species.

id_tips: Summer male is lemon yellow with a black cap and black wings marked in white. Female and winter birds are olive-tan with the same black-and-white wings and a small conical bill. Flight is bouncy.
habitat: Weedy fields, roadsides, and thistle feeders.
wnc: Common statewide. Numbers shift seasonally, and winter flocks are duller than the yellow summer males.
uses: Flight call is per-chick-o-ree, often given as the flock bounces overhead. Eats seeds, especially thistle, sunflower, and alder. Nests late, when seeds ripen.
caution: Native and protected. It is not the introduced House Finch, which is streaked and red rather than yellow.
lookalikes: House Finch and Purple Finch are streaked and never solid yellow with a black cap. Pine Siskin is streaked and has yellow only in the wings.
wikipedia_extract:
The American goldfinch (Spinus tristis) is a small North American bird in the finch family. It is migratory, ranging from mid-Alberta to North Carolina during the breeding season, and from just south of the Canada–United States border to Mexico during the winter.
The only finch in its subfamily to undergo a complete molt, the American goldfinch displays sexual dichromatism: the male is a vibrant yellow in the summer and an olive color during the winter, while the female is a dull yellow-brown shade which brightens only slightly during the summer. The male displays brightly colored plumage during the breeding season to attract a mate.
The American goldfinch is a granivore and adapted for the consumption of seedheads, with a conical beak to remove the seeds and agile feet to grip the stems of seedheads while feeding. It is a social bird and will gather in large flocks while feeding and mig

id_tips: Slate-gray or brownish hood and back, white belly, and white outer tail feathers that flash when it flies. Pink bill. The local mountain breeders are often darker; winter visitors vary.
habitat: Forest floors, feeders, and brushy edges. Breeds in high-elevation conifers and northern hardwoods.
wnc: Breeds in the higher mountains and winters commonly in yards across the whole state. A classic winter feeder bird in the piedmont.
uses: Song is a musical trill. Call is a dry tick and a twitter. Eats seeds and insects. Scratches on the ground under feeders.
caution: Native and protected. White tail edges and the pink bill separate it from sparrows and from the introduced House Sparrow.
lookalikes: Eastern Towhee is larger, with rusty sides and a red eye. Chickadees have a black bib and no white outer tail.
wikipedia_extract: The dark-eyed junco (Junco hyemalis) is a species of junco, a group of small, grayish New World sparrows. The species is common across much of temperate North America and in summer it ranges far into the Arctic. It is a variable species, much like the related fox sparrow (Passerella iliaca), and its systematics are still not completely resolved.

id_tips: Smallest woodpecker here. Black and white, with a white back stripe and white spots on the wings. The bill is short, about half the depth of the head. Males have a small red patch on the back of the head.
habitat: Woods, yards, and suet feeders. Often on small branches and weed stems.
wnc: The everyday woodpecker of yards and woods statewide, year-round.
uses: Call is a sharp pik, softer than a Hairy Woodpecker, and the whinny descends. Eats insects, and comes readily to suet.
caution: Native and protected. Suet is fine. Do not remove dead limbs that are being used as nest trees if you can leave them safely.
lookalikes: Hairy Woodpecker is larger, with a bill about as long as the head is deep, and a louder, sharper peek. The outer tail feathers of a Downy usually show black spots.
wikipedia_extract: The downy woodpecker (Dryobates pubescens) is a species of woodpecker, the smallest in North America. Length ranges from 14 to 18 cm (5.5 to 7.1 in). Downy woodpeckers primarily live in forested areas throughout the United States and Canada, with the exception of deserts in the southwest and the northern tundra. The bird nests in tree cavities and feeds primarily on insects, although it supplements its diet with seeds and berries. The downy woodpecker is very similar in appearance to the hairy woodpecker, although they are not closely related.

id_tips: Zebra-barred back and a red crown and nape. The male's red runs from the bill over the crown. The belly blush is faint and easy to miss. Pale face.
habitat: Hardwoods, yards, and feeders.
wnc: Common year-round in the piedmont, coastal plain, and lower mountains. Less common in the highest spruce-fir zone.
uses: Call is a rolling churr or quiver. Eats insects, acorns, fruit, and suet. Stores nuts in bark crevices.
caution: Native and protected. People often misname it Red-headed because of the red cap. The face is pale, not a solid red hood.
lookalikes: Red-headed Woodpecker has the entire head red and big white wing patches. Hairy and Downy are black and white without the barred back and red nape.
wikipedia_extract: The red-bellied woodpecker (Melanerpes carolinus) is a medium-sized woodpecker of the family Picidae. It breeds mainly in the eastern United States, ranging as far south as Florida and as far north as Canada. Though it has a vivid orange-red crown and nape it is not to be confused with the red-headed woodpecker, a separate species of woodpecker in the same genus with an entirely red head and neck that sports a solid black back and white belly.  The red-bellied earns its name from the pale reddish tint on its lower underside.

id_tips: Like a large Downy: white back, spotted wings, and a red nape patch on the male. The bill is long and chisel-like, nearly as long as the head is deep. Outer tail feathers are usually plain white.
habitat: Mature woods, including mountain forest. Less of a tiny-branch bird than the Downy.
wnc: Year-round in forests statewide, and a regular bird of mountain hardwoods and cove forest.
uses: Call is a loud, sharp peek. Drum is faster and more even than a Downy's. Eats wood-boring insects.
caution: Native and protected. Leave snags when they are safe. Those are nest and food trees.
lookalikes: Downy Woodpecker is smaller, with a short bill. If the bill looks longer than the head is deep, it is not a Downy.
wikipedia_extract: The hairy woodpecker (Leuconotopicus villosus) is a medium-sized woodpecker that is found over a large area of North America. It is approximately 250 mm (9.8 in) in length with a 380 mm (15 in) wingspan. With an estimated population in 2020 of almost nine million individuals, the hairy woodpecker is listed by the IUCN as a species of least concern. The species was previously placed in the genus Dryobates.

id_tips: Brown, barred above, spotted below, with a black crescent on the chest and a white rump that flashes in flight. Eastern birds show yellow under the wings and tail. Males have a black mustache.
habitat: Open woods, yards, and ants on lawns. Often feeds on the ground.
wnc: Common statewide. More widespread in winter in the lowlands, and a familiar mountain yard bird.
uses: Call is a loud kleer and a long wick-wick-wick. Eats ants and other insects more than any other local woodpecker.
caution: Native and protected. The white rump is the quick flight mark. It is not a dove.
lookalikes: No other local woodpecker is this brown and spotted with a white rump and yellow wing linings.
wikipedia_extract: The northern flicker or common flicker (Colaptes auratus) is a medium-sized bird of the woodpecker family. It is native to most of North America, parts of Central America, Cuba, and the Cayman Islands, and is one of the few woodpecker species that migrate. Over 100 common names for the northern flicker are known, including yellowhammer (not to be confused with the Eurasian yellowhammer (Emberiza citrinella)), clape, gaffer woodpecker, harry-wicket, heigh-ho, wake-up, walk-up, wick-up, yarrup, and gawker bird. Many of these names derive from attempts to imitate some of its calls.

id_tips: Crow-sized, black, with a big red crest and a white stripe down the neck. In flight the wings show white linings. Digs rectangular holes in dead wood.
habitat: Mature forest with large dead trees. Also wooded suburbs.
wnc: Widespread in forested North Carolina and especially noticeable in the mountains and big river swamps.
uses: Call is a loud, irregular kuk-kuk-kuk that carries through the woods. Eats carpenter ants and beetle larvae.
caution: Native and protected. The rectangular excavations are a sign of a living forest, not a reason to cut every snag.
lookalikes: A crow is all black and does not cling to trunks or show a red crest. Ivory-billed Woodpecker is not a bird you should expect to see.
wikipedia_extract: The pileated woodpecker ( PY-lee-ay-tid, PIL-ee-; Dryocopus pileatus) is a large, crow-sized woodpecker with a prominent red crest, white neck stripe, and a mostly black body. This woodpecker is native to North America, where it is the largest confirmed extant woodpecker species and the third-largest extant species of woodpecker in the world, after the great slaty woodpecker and the black woodpecker. It inhabits deciduous forests in eastern North America, the Great Lakes, the boreal forests of Canada, and parts of the Pacific Coast. This woodpecker is primarily an insectivore, eating insects that live in trees; it is famous for making large, nearly rectangular carvings into trees, which are used to extract prey inside the tree or to make a nest. The species has a large range and an increasing population, causing it to be categorized as a species of "least concern" by the IUCN.

id_tips: Blue-gray above, white face and breast, with a black or gray cap and a long thin bill. Creeps headfirst down trunks.
habitat: Mature deciduous woods and feeders.
wnc: Year-round in hardwoods across the state, including mountain coves.
uses: Call is a nasal yank-yank. Eats insects and seeds, and wedges them in bark. A regular suet and sunflower bird.
caution: Native and protected.
lookalikes: Brown-headed Nuthatch is smaller, has a brown cap, and prefers pines. Red-breasted Nuthatch has a black eye stripe and rusty underparts and is more of a conifer bird.
wikipedia_extract:
The white-breasted nuthatch (Sitta carolinensis) is a species of bird in the nuthatch family Sittidae. It is a medium-sized nuthatch, measuring approximately 15.5 cm (6.1 in) in length. Coloration varies somewhat along the species' range, but the upperparts are light blue-gray, with a black crown and nape in males, while females have a dark gray crown. The underparts are whitish, with a reddish tinge on the lower abdomen. Despite not being closely related, the white-breasted nuthatch and the white wagtail are very similar in plumage.
The white-breasted nuthatch is a chatty bird. It has a nasal voice and often utters little cries or vocalizations, often composed of repetitions of small invariant whistles. id_tips: Tiny. Brown cap, blue-gray back, white throat, and a pale spot on the nape. Bill is thin and slightly upturned. Almost always in pines.
habitat: Pine woods, including planted pines and pine-oak ridges.
wnc: A southeastern specialty. Common in coastal and piedmont pines and in lower-elevation mountain pines. Scarce in spruce-fir.
uses: Call sounds like a squeaky rubber toy. Eats insects and pine seeds. Nests in dead pine stubs and will use a small box.
caution: Native and protected. It depends on pines and small dead snags.
lookalikes: White-breasted Nuthatch is larger, white-faced, and has a black or gray cap, not a brown one.

The brown-headed nuthatch (Sitta pusilla) is a small songbird endemic to pine forests throughout the Southeastern United States. Genetic analyses indicated low differentiation between northern and southern populations in Florida, but the study also found  lower genetic diversity among south Florida populations that may be a result of the increased habitat fragmentation that was documented. The Bahama nuthatch was formerly considered a subspecies (S. p. insularis), but has since been reclassified as its own separate species. Two recent studies assessing vocalizations in Bahama and continental nuthatch populations found important differences.  One of the studies also demonstrated that  continental and Bahama populations did not respond aggressively to calls of the other population. This type of call-response study is often used to help define cryptic species.

id_tips: Tiny, brown-streaked above and white below, with a thin curved bill and a stiff tail. Spirals up a trunk, then flies to the base of the next tree.
habitat: Mature woods with rough bark. Easiest in winter.
wnc: Breeds sparingly in the high mountains and is a quiet winter visitor in woods statewide.
uses: Song is a thin, high see-see-see. Eats insects and spiders from bark crevices. Easy to overlook.
caution: Native and protected. If a brown streak seems to walk up the bark, stop and look. It is not a mouse.
lookalikes: Nuthatches go down trunks headfirst and are gray or brown-capped, not streaked brown. Woodpeckers hitch with the tail but are larger and patterned in black and white or barred brown.
wikipedia_extract: The brown creeper (Certhia americana), also known as the American treecreeper, is a small songbird, the only North American member of the treecreeper family Certhiidae.

id_tips: Tiny, blue-gray above and white below, with a white eye-ring and a long black tail edged in white. Constantly flicks the tail. Males show a thin black eyebrow in breeding season.
habitat: Deciduous treetops, river woods, and yards.
wnc: A common summer resident statewide, arriving in early spring. Does not stay through a mountain winter.
uses: Call is a thin, nasal spee. Song is a jumble of high notes. Eats tiny insects and spiders.
caution: Native and protected. A summer bird. A similar tiny gray bird in winter is more likely a kinglet.
lookalikes: Ruby-crowned and Golden-crowned Kinglets are greener, shorter-tailed, and present in winter. A cerulean warbler is blue but has wing bars and does not wag a long tail.
wikipedia_extract: The blue-gray gnatcatcher (Polioptila caerulea) is a very small gnatcatcher native to North America.

id_tips: Black and white, with a red forehead and a long white stripe on the wing. Males also have a red throat. Drills neat rows of sap wells in bark.
habitat: Orchards, yards, and deciduous woods in the cooler months. Breeds farther north and in high mountains.
wnc: A common winter woodpecker across the state. A few breed in the higher mountains.
uses: Call is a nasal mew. Drums in an irregular pattern. Eats sap, the insects attracted to it, and fruit.
caution: Native and protected. Rows of small holes are sap wells, not a sign that the tree must be cut.
lookalikes: Downy and Hairy Woodpeckers have a white back stripe, not a white wing panel, and they do not drill organized rows of wells.
wikipedia_extract: The yellow-bellied sapsucker (Sphyrapicus varius) is a medium-sized woodpecker that breeds in Canada and the northeastern United States.

id_tips: Male is black with a red shoulder edged in yellow, shown when he sings. Female is heavily streaked brown, with a pale eyebrow, and can show a dull reddish shoulder.
habitat: Marshes, pond edges, wet ditches, and winter blackbird flocks in fields.
wnc: Breeds in wetlands statewide, including mountain valleys, and forms large winter flocks in the lowlands.
uses: Song is a gurgling conk-la-ree. Eats insects in summer and grain and seeds in winter.
caution: Native and protected. Females are often mistaken for sparrows. Look for the larger size and the hint of a red shoulder.
lookalikes: Common Grackle is larger, longer-tailed, and lacks the red shoulder. European Starling is short-tailed and speckled, with no red epaulet.

The red-winged blackbird (Agelaius phoeniceus) is a passerine bird of the family Icteridae found in most of North America and much of Central America. It breeds from Alaska and Newfoundland south to Florida, the Gulf of Mexico, Mexico, and Guatemala, with isolated populations in western El Salvador, northwestern Honduras, and northwestern Costa Rica. It may winter as far north as Pennsylvania and British Columbia, but northern populations are generally migratory, moving south to Mexico and the Southern United States. 
Claims have been made that it is the most abundant living land bird in North America, as bird-counting censuses of wintering red-winged blackbirds sometimes show that loose flocks can number in excess of a million birds per flock and the full number of breeding pairs across North and Central America may exceed 250 million in peak years. id_tips: Male is glossy black with a brown head and a short, thick bill. Female is plain gray-brown, smaller than a blackbird, with a stout bill and faint streaking. Often walks near livestock.
habitat: Farms, feedlots, lawns, and forest edges.
wnc: Native to North America and now common statewide. It expanded east historically as forests were opened. It is not an introduced European species.
uses: Song is a liquid gurgle. Eats seeds and insects stirred up by cattle. Lays eggs in other birds' nests and does not raise its own young.
caution: Native, but brood parasitism hurts some songbirds. Do not destroy native songbird nests trying to remove eggs unless you are in a permitted research project.
lookalikes: The male's brown head separates it from grackles and Red-winged Blackbirds. Female cowbirds are plainer and thicker-billed than a female redwing.
wikipedia_extract: The brown-headed cowbird (Molothrus ater) is a small, obligate brood parasitic icterid native to temperate and subtropical North America. It is a permanent resident in the southern parts of its range; northern birds migrate to the southern United States and Mexico in winter, returning to their summer habitat around March or April.

id_tips: Chunky grassland bird with a bright yellow throat and breast and a black V on the chest. Streaked brown above. White outer tail feathers show when it flies. Often sings from a fence post.
habitat: Hayfields, pastures, and airports. Needs grass that is not mowed flat.
wnc: Still present in farmland across the state, but much reduced. More often heard than seen closely.
uses: Song is a clear, whistled spring-of-the-year. Eats insects and seeds. Nests on the ground.
caution: Native and declining. Early hay cutting destroys nests. It is not a Western Meadowlark, which is accidental in North Carolina.
lookalikes: Western Meadowlark looks almost the same. In North Carolina, a meadowlark is this species unless a careful listener hears the Western's lower, more complex song.
wikipedia_extract: The eastern meadowlark (Sturnella magna) is a medium-sized icterid bird, very similar in appearance to its sister species, the western meadowlark. It occurs from eastern North America to northern South America, where it is also most widespread in the east. The Chihuahuan meadowlark was formerly considered to be conspecific with the eastern meadowlark.

id_tips: Large, lanky, and glossy black with a purple or bronze sheen, a long keel-shaped tail, and a pale yellow eye. The bill is long and slightly curved.
habitat: Lawns, parking lots, marshes, and winter blackbird flocks.
wnc: Common statewide in towns and open country. Big flocks gather in the cooler months.
uses: Song is a harsh, creaking readle-eak. Eats insects, grain, acorns, and small animals. Walks on lawns with the tail held in a V.
caution: Native and protected, even though flocks are noisy and they raid feeders.
lookalikes: European Starling is smaller, short-tailed, and dark-eyed, with a yellow bill in summer. American Crow is heavier, all black including the eye, and fans a broader tail.
wikipedia_extract: The common grackle (Quiscalus quiscula) is an icterid bird found in large numbers through much of North America. It was first described in 1758 by Carl Linnaeus and has three officially recognized subspecies. Adult common grackles have a long and dark bill, pale yellow eyes, and a long tail. Adults often have a bluish iridescent appearance on their head, this feature being more pronounced on males. Common grackles can be found widely across North America east of the Rocky Mountains and are highly adaptable to their environment.

id_tips: A plover of dry ground. Brown above, white below, with two black breast bands, a red eye-ring, and a long tail with orange at the base. Loud and conspicuous.
habitat: Gravel lots, ball fields, pastures, and mudflats. Nests in a scrape on open ground.
wnc: Present statewide in open places, including mountain valleys and school fields. Many stay through mild winters.
uses: Call is its name, a shrill kill-deer. Eats insects and other invertebrates. Adults fake a broken wing to lead people from the nest.
caution: Native and protected. A bird fluttering on a gravel drive may be guarding eggs or chicks. Watch your step and move on.
lookalikes: No other common North Carolina bird has two complete black breast bands and that call. Semipalmated Plover has one breast band and sticks to mudflats.
wikipedia_extract: The killdeer (Charadrius vociferus) is a large plover found in the Americas. Its shrill, two-syllable call is often heard, sounding like "kill deer". It was described and given its current scientific name in 1758 by Carl Linnaeus in the 10th edition of his Systema Naturae. Three subspecies are described. Its upperparts are mostly brown with rufous fringes, the head has patches of white and black, and two black bands cross the breast. The belly and the rest of the breast are white. The nominate (or originally described) subspecies breeds from southeastern Alaska and southern Canada to Mexico. It is seen year-round in the southern half of its breeding range; the subspecies C. v. ternominatus is resident in the West Indies, and C. v. peruvianus inhabits Peru and surrounding South American countries throughout the year. North American breeders winter from their resident range south to Centra

id_tips: Large and dark, soaring with wings held in a shallow V. The trailing half of the wing is silvery. The head is small and red on adults, and the tail is long. Rocks unsteadily in flight.
habitat: Skies over roads, farms, and woods. Roosts on towers and dead trees.
wnc: Common statewide year-round, including the mountains. Often the first big soaring bird people notice.
uses: Almost silent. Finds carrion by smell as well as sight. Does not kill healthy livestock.
caution: Native and protected. A group on a roadkill is doing cleanup, not attacking pets.
lookalikes: Black Vulture has a shorter tail, pale silvery patches only at the wingtips, a gray head, and a flatter, snappier flight. Eagles soar on flat wings and have large feathered heads.

The turkey vulture (Cathartes aura) is the most widespread of the New World vultures. One of three species in the genus Cathartes of the family Cathartidae, the turkey vulture ranges from southern Canada to the southernmost tip of South America. It inhabits a variety of open and semi-open areas, including subtropical forests, shrublands, pastures, and deserts.
Like all New World vultures, it is not closely related to the Old World vultures of Europe, Africa, and Asia. However, the two groups strongly resemble each other due to convergent evolution.
The turkey vulture is a scavenger and feeds almost exclusively on carrion. It finds its food using its keen eyes and sense of smell, flying low enough to detect the gasses produced by the early stages of decay in dead animals. In flight, it uses thermals to move through the air, flapping its wings infrequently. It roosts in large community gro

id_tips: Black, with a short square tail and a gray, wrinkled head. In flight, white is limited to a patch at each wingtip. Flaps more often than a Turkey Vulture and holds the wings flatter.
habitat: Open country, dumps, and thermals. Often mixed with Turkey Vultures.
wnc: Common across the state and increasing. Regular in the mountains as well as the piedmont and coast.
uses: Quiet. Eats carrion and cannot smell it as well as a Turkey Vulture, so it often follows those birds to a carcass.
caution: Native and protected. It can occasionally peck at weak newborn livestock. That is a husbandry issue, not a reason to poison vultures.
lookalikes: Turkey Vulture shows silver along the whole rear of the wing, has a longer tail, and rocks in a V.
wikipedia_extract: The black vulture (Coragyps atratus), also known as the American black vulture, Mexican vulture, zopilote, urubu, or gallinazo, is a bird in the New World vulture family whose range extends from the northeastern United States to Peru, Central Chile and Uruguay in South America, and common throughout Brazil where it can be seen in large scavenging groups. Although a common and widespread species, it has a somewhat more restricted distribution than its compatriot, the turkey vulture, which breeds well into Canada and all the way south to Tierra del Fuego. It is the only extant member of the genus Coragyps, which is in the family Cathartidae. Despite the similar name and appearance, this species is not closely related to the Eurasian black vulture, an Old World vulture, of the family Accipitridae (which includes raptors like the eagles, hawks, kites, and harriers). id_tips: Broad-winged buteo. Adults have a brick-red tail. Most show a dark belly band on a pale chest and dark marks on the leading edge of the underwing. Often perches on roadside poles.
habitat: Fields, highways, and open woods.
wnc: The common soaring hawk of open country statewide, year-round. Mountain birds include darker western-looking visitors in winter.
uses: Call is a harsh screaming kee-eeer, the sound movies use for any raptor. Eats rodents, rabbits, and snakes.
caution: Native and protected. A hawk on a power pole is usually hunting rodents, not poultry.
lookalikes: Red-shouldered Hawk is more barred below, has crescent pale windows near the wingtips, and prefers woods. Cooper's Hawk has a long tail and short rounded wings.
wikipedia_extract:
The red-tailed hawk (Buteo jamaicensis) is a bird of prey and one of the most common hawks in North America. In the United States, it is one of three species colloquially known as the "chickenhawk". The red-tailed hawk breeds throughout most of the continent, from western Alaska and northern Canada to as far south as Panama and the West Indies. The red-tailed hawk occupies a wide range of habitats and altitudes, including deserts, grasslands, coniferous and deciduous forests, agricultural fields, and urban areas. It is absent in areas of unbroken forest and in the high arctic. It is legally protected in Canada, Mexico, and the United States by the Migratory Bird Treaty.
The red-tailed hawk is one of the largest members of the genus Buteo in North America, typically weighing from 690 to 1,600 g (1.5 to 3.5 lb) and measuring 45–65 cm (18–26 in) in length, with a wingspan from 110–145 cm (4

id_tips: Medium buteo of the woods. Adults are barred rusty below, with black-and-white checkered wings and a banded tail. In flight, translucent crescents near the wingtips.
habitat: River woods, swamps, and wooded suburbs.
wnc: A common resident of wet woods and neighborhoods across the state, including mountain valleys.
uses: Call is a repeated kee-aah, kee-aah, often given while soaring. Eats frogs, snakes, crayfish, and small mammals.
caution: Native and protected. The loud call over a yard is usually this hawk, not a jay, though Blue Jays imitate it.
lookalikes: Red-tailed Hawk has a red tail and a pale chest with a belly band, and it prefers more open country. Broad-winged Hawk is smaller, with a plainer wing and a shorter, banded tail, and it is mostly a summer bird.
wikipedia_extract: The red-shouldered hawk (Buteo lineatus) is a medium-sized buteo. Its breeding range spans eastern North America, along the coast of California and northern to northeastern-central Mexico. It is a permanent resident throughout most of its range, though northern birds do migrate, mostly to central Mexico. The main conservation threat to the widespread species is deforestation.

id_tips: A bird-hunting hawk with short rounded wings and a long rounded tail. Adults are gray above and rusty-barred below, with a dark cap. The tail tip looks rounded and usually shows a pale terminal band.
habitat: Woods and yards, especially bird feeders.
wnc: Now a common resident statewide, including towns. The scientific name was recently moved from Accipiter to Astur. Older guides still say Accipiter cooperii.
uses: Call near the nest is a loud kak-kak-kak. Eats birds. A sudden silence at the feeder often means one of these just came through.
caution: Native and protected. Taking a dove or a sparrow at a feeder is normal hunting, not a problem to solve by harming the hawk.
lookalikes: Sharp-shinned Hawk is smaller, with a more square-tipped tail and a thinner neck, and the male can be bluebird-small. Red-shouldered and Red-tailed Hawks have broad wings and shorter tails.
wikipedia_extract:
Cooper's hawk (Astur cooperii) is a medium-sized hawk native to the North American continent and found from southern Canada to Mexico. This species was formerly placed in the genus Accipiter.
As in many birds of prey, the male is smaller than the female. The birds found east of the Mississippi River tend to be larger on average than the birds found to the west. It is easily confused with the smaller but similar sharp-shinned hawk (Accipiter striatus).
The species was named in 1828 by Charles Lucien Bonaparte in honor of his friend and fellow ornithologist, William Cooper. Other common names for Cooper's hawk include: big blue darter, chicken hawk, flying cross, hen hawk, quail hawk, striker, and swift hawk. Many of the names applied to Cooper's hawks refer to their ability to hunt large and evasive prey using extremely well-developed agility.

id_tips: Smallest falcon here. Rusty back, blue-gray wings on the male, two black face stripes, and a habit of hovering over fields or sitting on a wire. Long pointed wings and a long tail.
habitat: Pastures, roadsides, and open country. Nests in cavities.
wnc: Present statewide in open land. More common in winter in some areas, and declining as a breeder.
uses: Call is a sharp klee-klee-klee. Eats insects, mice, and small birds. Hunts from wires and by hovering.
caution: Native and protected. It needs open grassland and nest cavities. It is not a sparrow.
lookalikes: Merlin is darker, streaked below, and lacks the rusty back and double face stripes. Sharp-shinned Hawk has rounded wings, not pointed falcon wings.
wikipedia_extract: The American kestrel (Falco sparverius) is the smallest and most common falcon in the Americas. Though it has been called the American "sparrow hawk", this now obsolete vernacular name is a misnomer; the American kestrel is a true falcon, while neither the Eurasian sparrowhawk nor the other species called sparrowhawks are in the family Falconidae, hence only very distantly related to the American kestrel. It has a roughly two-to-one range in size over subspecies and sex, varying in size from about the weight of a blue jay to a mourning dove. It is a very successful species, occurring almost throughout North and South America except for the Arctic fringes of North America, and the densest tropical Amazon rainforest areas; it has evolved into 17 subspecies adapted to different environments and habitats throughout the region. id_tips: Large, with a white head, a dark eye stripe, and dark brown above. The underside is mostly white with a dark wrist patch. Wings are long and crooked, like an M. Plunges feet-first for fish.
habitat: Lakes, rivers, reservoirs, and the coast. Nests on platforms, channel markers, and dead trees.
wnc: Summer resident at mountain lakes and rivers, and common on the piedmont reservoirs and the coast. Most leave in winter except along the coast.
uses: Call is a series of sharp whistles. Eats fish almost exclusively.
caution: Native and protected. A nest platform on a pole is often used for years. Give diving birds room in a boat.
lookalikes: Bald Eagle has a white head and tail and holds broad wings flat, and it snatches fish at the surface rather than plunging. A gull does not have the dark eye stripe and crooked wings.
wikipedia_extract:
The osprey (; Pandion haliaetus), historically known as sea hawk, river hawk, and fish hawk, is a diurnal, fish-eating bird of prey with a cosmopolitan range. It is a large raptor, reaching more than 60 cm (24 in) in length and a wingspan of 180 cm (71 in). It is brown on the upperparts and predominantly greyish on the head and underparts.
The osprey is distributed on all continents except Antarctica, but in South America, it occurs only as a nonbreeding migrant. It lives in a wide variety of habitats and nests in locations near a body of water providing an adequate food supply. It has specialised physical characteristics and unique behaviour in hunting its prey, which consists almost exclusively of fish.

id_tips: Huge. Adults have a white head and tail and a yellow bill. Immatures are dark brown and mottled and take four or five years to get the white head. Soars on flat, broad wings.
habitat: Large lakes, rivers, and the coast. Nests in big trees near water.
wnc: Recovered and now nests on lakes and rivers across the state, including some mountain reservoirs. Easiest along the coast and big piedmont lakes.
uses: Call is a thin series of whistles, not the red-tail scream used in films. Eats fish, waterbirds, and carrion.
caution: Native and protected. Give nests a wide berth in the breeding season.
lookalikes: Osprey is smaller, has a dark eye stripe, and shows a dark wrist patch under the wing. Turkey Vultures rock in a V and have tiny unfeathered heads.
wikipedia_extract:
The bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) is a bird of prey found in North America. A sea eagle, it has two known subspecies and forms a species pair with the white-tailed eagle (Haliaeetus albicilla), which occupies the same niche as the bald eagle in the Palearctic. Its range includes most of Canada and Alaska, all of the contiguous United States, and northern Mexico. It is found near large bodies of open water with an abundant food supply and old-growth trees for nesting.
The bald eagle is an opportunistic feeder that subsists mainly on fish, upon which it swoops down and snatches from the water with its talons. It builds the largest nest of any North American bird and the largest tree nests ever recorded for any animal species, up to 4 m (13 ft) deep, 2.5 m (8.2 ft) wide, and 1 metric ton (1.1 short tons) in weight. Sexual maturity is attained at the age of four to five years.

id_tips: Large, round-headed, and dark-eyed, with no ear tufts. Brown barring on the chest and streaks on the belly. Often calls in the daytime.
habitat: Mature woods, swamps, and wooded neighborhoods.
wnc: The common deep-woods owl of the state, including mountain coves. More often heard than seen.
uses: Call is who-cooks-for-you, who-cooks-for-you-all. Eats small mammals, frogs, and crayfish.
caution: Native and protected. If one answers your whistle, enjoy it and do not play calls for long. Repeated playback disturbs nesting birds.
lookalikes: Great Horned Owl has ear tufts and yellow eyes. Eastern Screech-Owl is much smaller and also yellow-eyed.
wikipedia_extract:
The barred owl (Strix varia), also known as the northern barred owl, striped owl or, more informally, hoot owl or eight hooter, is a North American large species of owl. A member of the true owl family, Strigidae, they belong to the genus Strix, which is also the origin of the family's name under Linnaean taxonomy. Barred owls are largely native to eastern North America, but have expanded their range to the west coast of North America where they are considered invasive. Mature forests are their preferred habitat, but they can also acclimatise to various gradients of open woodlands. Their diet consists mainly of small mammals, but this species is an opportunistic predator and is known to prey upon other small vertebrates such as birds, reptiles, and amphibians, as well as a variety of invertebrates.

id_tips: Very large, with ear tufts, yellow eyes, and a white throat bib. Mottled brown and gray. The classic hooting owl.
habitat: Woods edges, farms, and suburbs. Often uses an old hawk nest.
wnc: Resident statewide, from coastal woods to mountain ridges.
uses: Call is a deep hoo-h'HOO-hoo-hoo. Hunts at dusk and dawn. Eats mammals from mice to skunks, and birds.
caution: Native and protected. It can take free-ranging chickens at night. Housing the birds at night is the fix, not shooting the owl.
lookalikes: Barred Owl has no ear tufts and has dark eyes. A long-eared owl is much rarer and slimmer.
wikipedia_extract:
The great horned owl (Bubo virginianus), also known as the tiger owl (originally derived from early naturalists' description as the "winged tiger" or "tiger of the air") or the hoot owl, is a large owl native to the Americas. It is an extremely adaptable bird with a vast range and is the most widely distributed true owl in the Americas. Its diet consists primarily of rabbits and hares, rats and mice, and voles; it remains one of the few regular predators of skunk. Hunting also includes rodents, larger mid-sized mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and invertebrates. 
In ornithological study, the great horned owl is often compared to the Eurasian eagle-owl (Bubo bubo), a closely related species, which occupies the same ecological niche in Eurasia despite its notably larger size. id_tips: Tiny, green above, white below. Males have a ruby throat that can look black in poor light. Females have a white throat and white corners on the tail. Hovers at flowers.
habitat: Gardens, forest edges, and nectar feeders in the warm months.
wnc: The breeding hummingbird of North Carolina, common in summer from the coast to the mountains. Almost all are gone by late fall. A winter hummingbird is often a rare western species, not this one.
uses: Calls are high chips. Eats nectar and tiny insects. Feeders should be plain sugar water, one part sugar to four parts water, with no dye.
caution: Native and protected. Red dye is unnecessary. Change the sugar water before it ferments, especially in hot weather.
lookalikes: In summer in North Carolina, a hummingbird is this species. Rufous and other western hummingbirds show up rarely, mostly in fall and winter, and need a careful look.
wikipedia_extract: The ruby-throated hummingbird (Archilochus colubris) is a species of hummingbird that generally spends the winter in Central America, Mexico, and Florida, and migrates to Canada and other parts of Eastern North America for the summer to breed. It is the most common hummingbird in eastern North America, having population estimates of about 35 million in 2021.

id_tips: A cigar with wings. Dark gray-brown, with long narrow curved wings and a short tail. Flies with stiff, rapid flaps and never perches on a wire.
habitat: Skies over towns. Roosts and nests in chimneys.
wnc: A common summer bird statewide. Large evening flocks spiral into chimneys.
uses: Call is a high chitter overhead. Eats flying insects. Cannot perch normally. It clings to vertical walls.
caution: Native and protected. Capping a chimney during nesting season traps birds. Wait until the flock has migrated.
lookalikes: Swallows have broader triangular wings, perch on wires, and often show pale underparts. A bat has floppier flight and comes out later.

The chimney swift (Chaetura pelagica) is a bird belonging to the swift family Apodidae. A member of the genus Chaetura, it is closely related to both Vaux's swift and Chapman's swift; in the past, the three were sometimes considered to be conspecific. It has no subspecies. The chimney swift is a medium-sized, sooty gray bird with very long, slender wings and very short legs. Like all swifts, it is incapable of perching on flat surfaces, and can only perch on vertical surfaces. Many fly around all day and only come down at night when roosting.
The chimney swift feeds primarily on flying insects, but also on airborne spiders. It generally mates for life. id_tips: Steel blue above, orange-rust below and on the forehead, with a deeply forked tail and white tail spots. Flies low over fields and water.
habitat: Farms, bridges, and open country. Mud nests stuck to rafters and bridge beams.
wnc: A widespread summer resident, including mountain valleys with barns and bridges.
uses: Song is a twittering warble. Eats flying insects. The most familiar swallow of farms.
caution: Native and protected. A mud nest on a porch is a summer nest. It is empty after the birds leave.
lookalikes: Purple Martin is larger and the male is all dark. Tree Swallow is white below. Cliff Swallow has a square tail and a pale forehead.
wikipedia_extract:
The barn swallow (Hirundo rustica) is the most widespread species of swallow in the world, occurring on all continents, with vagrants reported even in Antarctica. It is a distinctive passerine bird with blue upperparts and a long, deeply forked tail. In Anglophone Europe, it is just called the swallow; in northern Europe, it is the only member of family Hirundinidae called a "swallow" rather than a "martin".
There are eight subspecies of barn swallow, which breed across the Northern Hemisphere. Two subspecies (H. r. savignii and H. r. transitiva) have fairly restricted ranges in the Nile valley and eastern Mediterranean, respectively. The other six are more widespread, with winter ranges covering much of the Southern Hemisphere.

id_tips: Largest swallow. Adult male is glossy blue-black all over. Female and young birds are dark above and dusky gray below, with a paler belly. Uses apartment houses and gourds in the East.
habitat: Open areas near water and towns, around martin houses.
wnc: Summer resident. More numerous in the piedmont and coastal plain than in the high mountains, but present in lower valleys.
uses: Calls are rich, liquid chirrups. Eats flying insects. In the East it depends on nest houses put up by people.
caution: Native and protected. European Starlings and House Sparrows take the compartments. A martin house needs to be managed, or those two will win.
lookalikes: Barn Swallow has a rusty belly and a forked tail. A male martin has no rust and no long tail streamers.
wikipedia_extract:
The purple martin (Progne subis) is a passerine bird in the swallow family Hirundinidae. It is the largest swallow in North America. They breed across the eastern United States and southeastern Canada, as well as the coastal Pacific Northwest, Baja California, Arizona, and New Mexico. Most make a brief stopover in the Yucatán Peninsula or Cuba during pre-breeding migration to North America and during post-breeding migration before reaching their overwintering sites in South America.
They are known for their speed, agility, and their characteristic mix of rapid, flapping, and gliding flight patterns. When approaching their nesting site, they will dive from the sky at great speeds with their wings tucked, just like the peregrine falcon does when hunting smaller birds.

id_tips: Plain gray-brown flycatcher with a dark head, no eye-ring, and no strong wing bars. Sits upright, wags its tail down, and says its name. Often nests on porch beams and bridges.
habitat: Streams, bridges, and woodland edges.
wnc: A common breeder statewide and one of the earliest spring migrants. Some winter in the piedmont and coastal plain.
uses: Song is a burry fee-bee, fee-b-be-bee. Eats flying insects. The tail wag and the song are the field marks.
caution: Native and protected. A mud-and-moss nest on a beam is this bird or a Barn Swallow. Phoebe nests are more cup-shaped and mossy.
lookalikes: Eastern Wood-Pewee has wing bars and a plainer head and sings pee-a-wee. Empidonax flycatchers have eye-rings and are best named by song.
wikipedia_extract: The eastern phoebe (Sayornis phoebe) is a small passerine bird. The genus name Sayornis is constructed from the specific part of Charles Lucien Bonaparte's name for Say's phoebe, Muscicapa saya, and Ancient Greek ornis, "bird". Phoebe is an alternative name for the Roman moon goddess Diana, but it may also have been chosen to imitate the bird's call.

id_tips: Pot-bellied thrush, warm rusty-brown on the head, with bold round black spots on a white breast and a white eye-ring. Larger than a bluebird.
habitat: Mature deciduous forest with a leafy floor.
wnc: A signature summer voice of mountain coves and also of piedmont woods. Winters in Central America.
uses: Song is a flutelike ee-oh-lay, with phrases that seem to harmonize. Eats insects and fruit from the forest floor.
caution: Native and declining. Forest fragmentation lets cowbirds find its nests. Keeping large woods intact helps it.
lookalikes: Brown Thrasher is longer-billed, longer-tailed, streaked rather than round-spotted, and yellow-eyed. Hermit Thrush is smaller, with a rusty tail and finer spots, and is mostly a winter bird here.
wikipedia_extract:
The wood thrush (Hylocichla mustelina) is a North American passerine bird in the family Turdidae and is the only species placed in the genus Hylocichla. It is closely related to other thrushes such as the American robin and is widely distributed across North America, wintering in Central America and southern Mexico. The wood thrush is the official bird of the District of Columbia.
The wood thrush is a medium-sized thrush, with brown upper parts with mottled brown and white underparts. The male and female are similar in appearance. The song of the male is often cited as being the most beautiful in North America.
The wood thrush is an omnivore, and feeds preferentially on soil invertebrates and larvae, but will also eat fruits. In the summer, it feeds on insects continuously in order to meet daily metabolic needs. It is solitary, but sometimes forms mixed-species flocks. The wood thrush de

id_tips: Breeding male is scarlet with black wings and tail. Female is yellow-olive with darker wings. The bill is thick but not huge. A treetop bird.
habitat: Mature deciduous forest in summer.
wnc: A common summer resident of mountain hardwoods and also of larger piedmont woods. Gone in winter.
uses: Song sounds like a robin with a sore throat, a burry carol. Call is a chick-burr. Eats insects and fruit.
caution: Native and protected. The male's red is a summer plumage. In fall he molts to olive with black wings.
lookalikes: Summer Tanager is all red, including the wings, and has a larger pale bill. Northern Cardinal has a crest and a black mask.

The scarlet tanager (Piranga olivacea) is a medium-sized American songbird in the cardinal family (Cardinalidae). It was placed in the tanager family (Thraupidae) until 2009, but was moved to Cardinalidae following several genetic studies indicating the Piranga tanagers are more closely related to cardinals and their allies. Breeding males have bright red plumage with black wings and tails, while females are yellow-olive. Outside the breeding season, males develop plumage similar to that of females, although their wings and tails remain darker. 
The species breeds mainly in large deciduous forests in eastern North America. It migrates through Central America to spend the winter in forests along the Andean foothills of northwestern South America. id_tips: Breeding male looks deep blue all over, with a small conical bill. In poor light he looks black. Female is plain warm brown with faint streaks and a hint of blue in the tail.
habitat: Brushy edges, powerlines, and old fields. Sings from a high perch.
wnc: One of the most common summer birds of shrubby places statewide, including mountain roadsides.
uses: Song is a paired series of sweet notes, often described as fire-fire, where-where, here-here. Eats seeds and insects.
caution: Native and protected. A black-looking bird on a wire that sings a paired song is often this bunting, not a cowbird.
lookalikes: Eastern Bluebird has a rusty breast and a thinner bill. Blue Grosbeak is larger, with chestnut wing bars and a huge bill.
wikipedia_extract:
The indigo bunting (Passerina cyanea) is a small seed-eating bird in the cardinal family, Cardinalidae. It is migratory, ranging from southern Canada to northern Florida during the breeding season, and from southern Florida to northern South America during the winter. It often migrates by night, using the stars to navigate. Its habitat is farmland, brush areas, and open woodland. The indigo bunting is closely related to the lazuli bunting and interbreeds with the species where their ranges overlap.
The indigo bunting is a small bird, measuring 11.5–13 cm (4.5–5.1 in) in length. It displays sexual dimorphism in its coloration; the male is vibrant blue in the summer, with brightly colored  plumage during the breeding season to attract a mate. id_tips: Olive above, white below, with a gray cap, a white eyebrow bordered by black, and a red eye that is hard to see. Bill has a tiny hook.
habitat: Deciduous treetops.
wnc: An abundant summer resident of hardwoods statewide. One of the most numerous forest birds in the mountains.
uses: Song is a endless series of short robin-like questions, here-I-am, where-are-you, sung all day. Eats caterpillars and other insects.
caution: Native and protected. If the woods seem full of a questioning song in June, it is often this bird.
lookalikes: White-eyed Vireo is smaller, yellow-spectacled, and sticks to thickets. Blue-headed Vireo has a blue-gray head, white spectacles, and wing bars.
wikipedia_extract:
The red-eyed vireo (Vireo olivaceus) is a small American songbird. It is somewhat warbler-like but not closely related to the New World warblers (Parulidae). Common across its vast range, this species is not considered threatened by the IUCN.
Vireo is a Latin word referring to a green migratory bird, perhaps the female golden oriole, possibly the European greenfinch. The specific olivaceus is Neo-Latin for 'olive-green', from Latin oliva ('olive').

id_tips: A warbler that walks on the ground like a tiny thrush. Olive-brown above, spotted below, with a bold white eye-ring and an orange crown stripe bordered in black.
habitat: Deciduous forest floor. The nest is a domed oven of leaves on the ground.
wnc: A common summer breeder in mountain and piedmont hardwoods.
uses: Song is an emphatic teacher, teacher, teacher, growing louder. Eats insects from the leaf litter.
caution: Native and protected. The nest is on the ground. Watch where you step on off-trail forest floor in May and June.
lookalikes: Louisiana and Northern Waterthrushes also walk and are streaked, but they bob the tail and lack the orange crown. Wood Thrush is much larger.
wikipedia_extract:
The ovenbird (Seiurus aurocapilla) is a small songbird of the New World warbler family Parulidae. It is the only species placed in the genus Seiurus. This migratory bird breeds in eastern North America and winters in Central America, many Caribbean islands, Florida and northern Venezuela.
Despite its name, it is not in the ovenbird family of birds.

id_tips: Yellow face and underparts. The male has a black hood and black throat framing the yellow face. Female shows at least a shadow of the hood. White in the outer tail, flicked open.
habitat: Shrubby understory of moist deciduous woods.
wnc: A characteristic summer warbler of southern forests, common in the mountains and piedmont.
uses: Song is a loud weeta-weeta-wee-tee-o. Eats insects. Often low in the shrubs, unlike many treetop warblers.
caution: Native and protected. A yellow warbler with a black cowl in a mountain rhododendron thicket is this bird.
lookalikes: Kentucky Warbler has a black mustache and a yellow eyebrow, and it stays on the ground. Wilson's Warbler has a black cap, not a full hood, and is a migrant here.
wikipedia_extract:
The hooded warbler (Setophaga citrina) is a New World warbler. It breeds in eastern North America across the eastern United States and into southernmost Canada (Ontario). It is migratory, wintering in Central America and the West Indies. Hooded warblers are very rare vagrants to western Europe.
Recent genetic research has suggested that the type species of Wilsonia (hooded warbler W. citrina) and of Setophaga (American redstart S. ruticilla) are closely related and should be merged into the same genus. As the name Setophaga (published in 1827) takes priority over Wilsonia (published in 1838), hooded warbler would then be transferred as Setophaga citrina. This change has been accepted by the North American Classification Committee of the American Ornithologists' Union, and the IOC World Bird List. The South American Classification Committee continues to list the bird in the genus Wilsonia

id_tips: Olive-yellow with two white wing bars and a fairly plain face. Males are brighter yellow on the throat and breast. Almost always in pines. A stout bill for a warbler.
habitat: Pine woods, including winter mixed flocks.
wnc: Year-round in much of the coastal plain and piedmont. In the mountains it is a breeder in pine stands and less common in winter.
uses: Song is a musical trill, sweeter and slower than a Chipping Sparrow. Eats insects and, in winter, seeds. One of the few warblers that comes to suet.
caution: Native and protected. A yellow bird in a pine in January is often this warbler, not a goldfinch.
lookalikes: Yellow-throated Vireo is brighter yellow on the spectacles and throat and sings short phrases. American Goldfinch has a conical bill and black wings.
wikipedia_extract: The pine warbler (Setophaga pinus) is a small songbird of the New World warbler family Parulidae. It is a permanent resident in the southeastern United States and also breeds in southeastern Canada and the northeastern United States, where it is migratory. Unlike other wood-warblers, in addition to insects the pine warbler also sometimes consumes seeds.
