id_tips: In winter, gray-brown with a yellow rump, yellow sides, and a broken white eye-ring. Breeding males are blue-gray with a black mask and the same yellow rump. Often in flocks.
habitat: Wax myrtle, bayberry, yards, and woodland edges in the cooler months.
wnc: The common winter warbler across the state. A few of the mountain forests see them as migrants. They largely leave by late spring.
uses: Call is a loud check. Eats insects and, in winter, wax-myrtle and other berries. More cold-hardy than other warblers.
caution: Native and protected. The yellow rump is the mark when the rest of the bird looks dull.
lookalikes: Pine Warbler is more yellow-olive and stays in pines. Palm Warbler bobs its tail and has yellow under the tail.
wikipedia_extract:
The yellow-rumped warbler (Setophaga coronata) is a North American bird species that can be commonly observed all across the continent. Its extensive range connects both the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of the U.S. as well as Canada and Central America, with the population concentrated in the continent's northern reaches during the breeding season and migrating southwards to southern North and Central America in the winter. It generally prefers coniferous forests or mixed coniferous-deciduous forests as its breeding habitat, while during the winter it can be found inhabiting more open areas such as shrublands that offer food resources. The yellow-rumped warbler is primarily insectivorous, though the species eats fruit such as juniper berries, especially in winter.

id_tips: Streaked black and white all over, including a striped crown. Creeps along branches and trunks like a nuthatch. The bill is thin and slightly curved.
habitat: Deciduous and mixed woods.
wnc: A common spring migrant and summer breeder in mountain and piedmont woods. Winters mostly farther south, with a few on the coast.
uses: Song is a thin, squeaky wee-see, wee-see, wee-see. Eats insects from bark.
caution: Native and protected. It is a warbler, not a woodpecker or a nuthatch, despite the creeping habit.
lookalikes: Blackpoll Warbler males have a solid black cap and white cheeks, and they do not creep. Nuthatches are blue-gray or brown-capped and have straight, thicker bills.
wikipedia_extract: The black-and-white warbler (Mniotilta varia) is a species of New World warbler, and the only member of its genus, Mniotilta. It breeds in northern and eastern North America and winters in Florida, Central America, and the West Indies down to Peru. It has been recorded as a vagrant in Northern Europe, especially Britain and Ireland. Relative to other New World warblers, it is not well studied.

id_tips: Male is olive above and yellow below with a black mask edged above in white. Female is olive and yellow with no mask, and a pale eye-ring. Skulks low in wet brush.
habitat: Marshes, wet thickets, and ditch edges.
wnc: A common summer bird of wet brush statewide, including mountain seeps. A few winter on the coast.
uses: Song is witchety-witchety-witchety. Call is a dry chip. Eats insects.
caution: Native and protected. The black mask in a cattail patch is the male.
lookalikes: Kentucky Warbler has a yellow eyebrow and a black mustache and lives in forest understory, not open marsh. Hooded Warbler has a full black hood, not just a mask, and flicks white tail spots.
wikipedia_extract: The common yellowthroat (Geothlypis trichas) is a New World warbler. It is an abundant breeder in North America, ranging from southern Canada to central Mexico. In the northern parts of its range the birds are migratory, wintering in the southern parts of the breeding range, Central America and the West Indies. Southern forms are largely resident. Historically, it has also been known as the "yellow bandit", Maryland yellow-throat, and yellow-breasted warbler.

id_tips: Slate gray all over, with a black cap and a chestnut patch under the tail. Slender, and often hidden in shrubs.
habitat: Thickets, hedgerows, and yards.
wnc: A common summer resident statewide. A few winter on the coast.
uses: Call is a nasal mew like a cat. Song is a long ramble of phrases, each given once, not repeated the way a mockingbird does. Eats insects and fruit.
caution: Native and protected.
lookalikes: Northern Mockingbird is paler gray, with white wing patches and white outer tail feathers, and no black cap. Brown Thrasher is rusty and streaked.
wikipedia_extract: The gray catbird (Dumetella carolinensis), also spelled grey catbird, is a medium-sized North American and Central American perching bird of the mimid family. It is the only member of the "catbird" genus Dumetella. Like the black catbird (Melanoptila glabrirostris), it is among the basal lineages of the Mimidae, probably a closer relative of the Caribbean thrasher and trembler assemblage than of the mockingbirds and Toxostoma thrashers. In some areas it is known as the slate-colored mockingbird.

id_tips: Rusty-brown above, heavily streaked below, with a long curved bill, a long tail, and yellow eyes. Spends time on the ground in thickets.
habitat: Hedgerows, field edges, and dense yards.
wnc: A common breeder statewide and the state bird's neighbor in thickets. Many withdraw from the high mountains in winter.
uses: Song is a long series of phrases, each usually doubled. Eats insects, and also fruit. Sings from the top of a shrub.
caution: Native and protected. It is not a Wood Thrush. The yellow eye, long bill, and streaks rather than round spots separate them.
lookalikes: Wood Thrush has round spots, a short bill, and a white eye-ring, and it stays in forest. A mockingbird is gray, not rusty.
wikipedia_extract:
The brown thrasher (Toxostoma rufum), sometimes erroneously called the brown thrush or fox-coloured thrush, is a bird in the family Mimidae, which also includes the New World catbirds and mockingbirds. The brown thrasher is abundant throughout the eastern and central United States and southern and central Canada, and it is the only thrasher to live primarily east of the Rockies and central Texas. It is the state bird of Georgia.
As a member of the genus Toxostoma, the bird is relatively large-sized among the other thrashers. It has brown upper parts with a white under part with dark streaks. Because of this, it is often confused with the smaller wood thrush (Hylocichla mustelina), among other species. The brown thrasher is noted for having over 1,000 song types, and the largest song repertoire of birds. However, each note is usually repeated in two or three phrases.

id_tips: Sleek and crested, tan and gray, with a black mask, a yellow tail tip, and sometimes red waxy tips on the wing feathers. Almost always in a flock.
habitat: Fruiting trees, orchards, and riversides.
wnc: Present year-round in the state, but flocks wander. Common in the mountains when berries and cherries are ripe, and widespread in winter.
uses: Call is a thin, high seee. Eats fruit for much of the year, and insects in summer. Can pass berries beak to beak.
caution: Native and protected. Fermented fruit can make a flock clumsy. That is temporary. Do not try to 'rescue' every bird unless it is in a road.
lookalikes: Tufted Titmouse is gray and crested but much smaller, with a black forehead and no black mask or yellow tail tip.
wikipedia_extract: The cedar waxwing (Bombycilla cedrorum) is a member of the family Bombycillidae or waxwing family of passerine birds. It is a medium-sized bird that is mainly brown, gray, and yellow. Some of the wing feathers have red tips, which resemble sealing wax, giving the bird its common name. It is a native of North and Central America, breeding in open wooded areas in southern Canada and wintering in the southern half of the United States, Central America, and the far northwest of South America. Its diet includes cedar cones, fruit, holly berries, and insects. The cedar waxwing is listed as least concern on the IUCN Red List.

id_tips: Blackish above, white below, with a white band at the tip of the tail. Sits upright on wires and chases crows and hawks.
habitat: Fields, ponds, and orchards with perches.
wnc: A common summer bird of open country statewide, including mountain valleys.
uses: Call is a sharp sputtering dzee. Eats flying insects and some fruit. Fearless around larger birds near the nest.
caution: Native and protected. The white tail band is the mark when it flies off a fence.
lookalikes: Eastern Phoebe is smaller, plainer, and wags its tail, and it lacks the white tail tip. A shrike has a hooked bill and a black mask.
wikipedia_extract: The eastern kingbird (Tyrannus tyrannus) is a large tyrant flycatcher native to the Americas. The bird is predominantly dark gray with white underbelly and pointed wings. Eastern kingbirds are conspicuous and are commonly found in open areas with scattered trees and bushes, where they perch while foraging for insects. The Eastern kingbird is migratory, with its breeding range spread across North America and its wintering range in Central and South America.

id_tips: Male is rose-red all over, including the wings, with no crest and no black mask. Female is mustard yellow. The bill is large and pale. Young males can be blotched red and yellow.
habitat: Open pine-oak woods and yards in summer.
wnc: A southern summer bird. Common in the piedmont and coastal plain and in the lower mountains. Scarcer in the highest hardwood coves, where Scarlet Tanager takes over.
uses: Song is a robin-like carol, sweeter than a Scarlet Tanager's. Call is a distinctive pick-i-tuck. Eats bees and wasps as well as other insects.
caution: Native and protected. An all-red bird with no crest is this tanager or, if the wings are black, a Scarlet Tanager.
lookalikes: Scarlet Tanager males have black wings. Northern Cardinal has a crest and a black face. A male House Finch is red only on the head and breast and is streaked brown on the sides.
wikipedia_extract: The summer tanager (Piranga rubra) is a medium-sized American songbird. Formerly placed in the tanager family (Thraupidae), it and other members of its genus are now classified in the cardinal family (Cardinalidae). The species's plumage and vocalizations are similar to other members of the cardinal family.

id_tips: Big brown goose with a black neck and head and a white chinstrap. The tail and rump show white. Flocks fly in a V and honk.
habitat: Ponds, golf courses, parks, and winter fields.
wnc: Native. Migrants pass through, and many resident flocks now stay year-round on lakes and lawns across the state, including some mountain lakes. Those resident birds descend partly from stocked flocks.
uses: Call is the familiar honk. Eats grass, waste grain, and aquatic plants.
caution: Native and protected. Do not feed them bread. It crowds parks and is poor food. A hissing bird at a nest will strike. Give it room.
lookalikes: A white farm goose is a domestic bird, not this one. Snow Goose is white or blue-gray and lacks the black neck and chinstrap. Brant is a small coastal goose and is rare inland.
wikipedia_extract:
The Canada goose (Branta canadensis) is a large species of goose with a black head and neck, white cheeks, white under its chin, and a brown body. It is native to the Arctic and temperate regions of North America, and it is occasionally found during migration across the Atlantic in northern Europe. It has been introduced to France, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Scandinavia, New Zealand, Japan, Chile, Argentina, and the Falkland Islands. Like most geese, the Canada goose is primarily herbivorous and normally migratory; often found on or close to fresh water, the Canada goose is also common in brackish marshes, estuaries, and lagoons.

habitat: Ponds, parks, rivers, and marshes.
wnc: Native and now the common duck of park ponds statewide, including the mountains. Wild migrants also occur. Many park birds are tame descendants of released stock.
uses: Female gives the classic quack. Male's call is quieter. Eats aquatic plants, seeds, and invertebrates.
caution: Native and protected, including most park birds. Do not feed bread. Loose domestic ducks may be white or piebald and are not a separate wild species.
lookalikes: American Black Duck is darker, with a plainer face and an olive bill, and is more of a coastal marsh duck. Mottled female mallards are the ones people call 'brown ducks.'

The mallard () or wild duck (Anas platyrhynchos) is a dabbling duck that breeds throughout the temperate and subtropical Americas, Eurasia, and North Africa. It has been introduced to New Zealand, Australia, Peru, Brazil, Uruguay, Argentina, Chile, Colombia, the Falkland Islands, and South Africa. Belonging to the subfamily Anatinae of the waterfowl family Anatidae, mallards live in wetlands, eat water plants and small animals, and are social animals preferring to congregate in groups or flocks of varying sizes.
Males (drakes) have green heads, while the females (ducks) have mainly brown-speckled plumage. Both sexes have an area of white-bordered black or iridescent purple or blue feathers called a speculum on their wings; males especially tend to have blue speculum feathers. id_tips: Male is unmistakable: crested green-purple head, red eye, white throat stripes, chestnut breast, and buffy sides. Female is gray-brown with a white tear-shaped eye patch and a small crest.
habitat: Wooded swamps, beaver ponds, and quiet creeks. Nests in tree cavities and boxes.
wnc: A common breeding duck of wooded water statewide, including mountain beaver ponds.
uses: Female's call is a rising squeal, oo-eek. Eats seeds, acorns, and aquatic insects. Ducklings jump from the nest cavity to the ground.
caution: Native and protected. A nest box over water helps. Leave the box up year-round and don't open it while a hen is incubating.
lookalikes: No other North Carolina duck has the male's painted pattern. The female's white teardrop eye patch separates her from a female Mallard.
wikipedia_extract: The wood duck or Carolina duck (Aix sponsa) is a partially migratory species of perching duck found in North America. The male is one of the most colorful North American waterfowls.

id_tips: Tall gray-blue heron with a long yellow bill, a black stripe over the eye, and slow, deep wingbeats. Neck folds in an S in flight. Stands still in the shallows.
habitat: Rivers, ponds, marshes, and even wet pastures.
wnc: The widespread heron of the state, year-round on unfrozen water, including mountain rivers.
uses: Call is a harsh frank when flushed. Eats fish, frogs, and the occasional small mammal.
caution: Native and protected. It is not a crane. Cranes fly with the neck straight out. This bird folds the neck.
lookalikes: Great Egret is all white. Sandhill Crane is grayer, red-crowned, and flies with the neck out. A tricolored heron is smaller and more coastal.
wikipedia_extract: The great blue heron (Ardea herodias) is a large wading bird in the heron family (Ardeidae), common near shores of open water and wetlands over most of North and Central America, as well as Northwestern South America, the Caribbean, and the Galápagos Islands. It is occasionally found in the Azores and is a rare vagrant to Europe. An all-white population found in South Florida, the Florida Keys, and the Caribbean islands, is known as the great white heron. Debate exists about whether these white birds are a color morph of the great blue heron, a subspecies of it, or an entirely separate species.

habitat: Rivers, ponds, and coasts with banks for nest tunnels.
wnc: Present along water statewide. Mountain birds may move downstream when creeks freeze.
uses: Call is a loud dry rattle. Eats fish and crayfish. Nests in a burrow in a dirt bank.
caution: Native and protected. The female is the one with the extra rusty belt. That is the reverse of many birds.
lookalikes: Blue Jays are blue and crested but have a black necklace, white wing spots, and do not plunge into water.
wikipedia_extract: The belted kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon) is a large, conspicuous water kingfisher, native to North America.

id_tips: Small, dark heron. Back looks green-black, neck is chestnut, and the legs are yellow-orange. Often hunched on a log. Stretches the neck when alarmed.
habitat: Pond edges, creeks, and marshes.
wnc: A common summer heron statewide, including small mountain ponds. Most leave in winter.
uses: Call is a sharp skeow. Eats fish and will sometimes drop a feather or insect as bait.
caution: Native and protected. It is much smaller than a Great Blue Heron and easy to miss until it flushes.
lookalikes: Least Bittern is even smaller, buff and black, and hides in reeds. American Bittern is streaked brown and larger.

The green heron (Butorides virescens) is a small heron of North and Central America. Butorides is from Middle English butor "bittern" and Ancient Greek -oides, "resembling", and virescens is Latin for "greenish".
It was long considered conspecific with its sister species the striated heron (Butorides striata); when treated together, they were called "green-backed heron".

id_tips: Tall and entirely white, with a yellow bill and black legs. Neck folds in flight. Breeding birds grow long plumes on the back.
habitat: Marshes, tidal creeks, ponds, and wet fields.
wnc: Common on the coast and piedmont. Wanders up rivers and to mountain lakes, especially after the breeding season.
uses: Mostly quiet away from the colony. Eats fish and frogs. Colonies are in trees over water.
caution: Native and protected. Plume hunting nearly wiped egrets out a century ago. Give rookeries distance.
lookalikes: Snowy Egret is smaller, with a black bill, black legs, and yellow feet. A white immature Little Blue Heron has a gray bill tipped in black and greenish legs. Cattle Egret is stockier and often buff-stained.
wikipedia_extract: The great egret (Ardea alba), also known as the common egret, large egret, great white egret, or great white heron, is a large, widely distributed egret.  The four subspecies are found in Asia, Africa, the Americas, and southern Europe. Recently, it has also been spreading to more northern areas of Europe. Distributed across most of the tropical and warmer temperate regions of the world, it builds tree nests in colonies close to water.

id_tips: Black waterbird with a long neck, a hooked bill, and orange facial skin. Sits low in the water and holds the wings out to dry. Flies in lines with the neck stretched.
habitat: Lakes, rivers, and the coast.
wnc: Common on the coast and on inland lakes. Regular at piedmont reservoirs and seen on larger mountain lakes. Older guides call it Phalacrocorax auritus.
uses: Mostly silent away from colonies. Dives for fish.
caution: Native and protected. It is not a duck and it is not an invasive snakebird. Anhingas are more southern and coastal and have a pointed bill and a fan tail.
lookalikes: Anhinga has a snakier neck, a straight pointed bill, and silver wing patches. A loon is lower, dagger-billed, and does not perch upright on pilings with wings spread.
wikipedia_extract: The double-crested cormorant (Nannopterum auritum) is a member of the cormorant family of water birds. It is found near rivers and lakes and in coastal areas and is widely distributed across North America, from the Aleutian Islands in Alaska down to Florida and Mexico. Measuring 70–90 cm (28–35 in) in length, it is entirely black except for a bare patch of orange-yellow facial skin and some extra plumage that it exhibits in the breeding season when it grows a double crest in which black feathers are mingled with white. Five subspecies are recognized. It mainly eats fish and hunts by swimming and diving. Its feathers, like all cormorants, are not waterproof, and it must dry them out after spending time in the water. Once threatened by the use of DDT, the numbers of this bird have increased markedly in recent years.

id_tips: Huge white swan with an orange bill and a black knob at the base of the bill. The neck is often held in an S. Wings are sometimes arched over the back.
habitat: Park ponds, coastal bays, and lakes. Many North Carolina birds are escapes or wanderers.
wnc: Introduced from Europe. The N.C. Wildlife Resources Commission says there is no established wild breeding population in the state. Birds show up as released pets or visitors from farther north. Do not treat one as a native breeding swan.
uses: Not mute. It hisses and grunts. Eats submerged plants. Can be aggressive near a nest.
caution: Introduced, and not protected as a native migratory swan. A territorial adult can injure a person or a dog. Do not feed it, and do not confuse it with a Tundra Swan.
lookalikes: Tundra Swan has a black bill, often with a small yellow spot, and holds the neck straighter. Trumpeter Swan is a rare visitor with an all-black bill and no yellow spot. Domestic white geese are smaller and have knobs or orange bills without the swan shape.
wikipedia_extract: The mute swan (Cygnus olor) is a species of swan and a member of the family Anatidae within the waterfowl order. It is native to much of Europe and parts of Asia and (as a rare winter visitor) the far north of Africa. It is an introduced species in North America, home to the largest populations outside of its native range, with additional smaller introductions in Australasia and Southern Africa. The name "mute" derives from it being less vocal than other swan species. Typically measuring 140 to 160 cm (55 to 63 in) in length, this large swan is wholly white in plumage, with an orange beak bordered with black. It is recognisable by its pronounced knob atop the beak, which is larger in males.

id_tips: Large white swan with a black bill. Many adults show a small yellow spot in front of the eye. The neck is long and usually held straighter than a Mute Swan's. No orange bill and no knob.
habitat: Coastal bays, refuges, and winter fields. Flocks fly in lines and call.
wnc: Native. Large numbers winter on the northeastern coastal plain, especially pocosin lakes and refuges. Rare in the mountains. This is the wild swan of North Carolina.
uses: Call is a mellow hoop or whooping, given by flocks. Eats aquatic plants and waste grain in winter fields.
caution: Native and protected. If you see a swan flock on the coast in winter, it is this species unless a bird shows an orange knobbed bill.
lookalikes: Mute Swan has the orange bill and black knob and is usually alone or in a park pair. Trumpeter Swan lacks the yellow spot and is a rare visitor.
wikipedia_extract:
The tundra swan (Cygnus columbianus) is a species of swan which breeds in the arctic, and overwinters in North America, Europe, and Asia. It is the smallest of the Holarctic swans, at 115–150 cm (45–59 in) in length, 168–211 cm (66–83 in) in wingspan and 3.4–9.6 kg (7.5–21.2 lb) in weight. Typically, the plumage of adults is entirely white, with solid black feet, a black beak that has varying amounts of yellow, and a thin streak of pink along the mouthline, although colour variation is common.
In the summer, they mainly eat aquatic vegetation, while at other times of year they often eat leftover crops, such as potatoes. They have few natural predators, although sometimes Arctic foxes, parasitic jaegers, and glaucous gulls will prey upon their eggs and chicks. Their main cause of death is poaching. During the breeding season, tundra swans become aggressive, and may attack passing animals

id_tips: Huge dark bird with a bare red-and-blue head. Males show a beard on the chest and fan a bronze tail. Females are smaller and duller. Flies up to roost in trees, despite the size.
habitat: Oak woods, fields, and forest edges.
wnc: Native and restored. Now common in woods and farm edges across the state, including the mountains.
uses: Male gobbles in spring. Eats acorns, seeds, and insects. A regulated game bird.
caution: Native. Hunting is by season and license only. A flock in a yard is wild, not a lost farm bird, unless the plumage is white.
lookalikes: Domestic turkeys are heavier, often white or piebald, and stay near barns. Ruffed Grouse is much smaller and crested, and it drums rather than gobbles.
wikipedia_extract: The wild turkey (Meleagris gallopavo) is an upland game bird native to North America, one of two extant species of turkey and the heaviest member of the order Galliformes. It is the ancestor to the domestic turkey (M. g. domesticus), which was originally derived from a southern Mexican subspecies of wild turkey (not the related ocellated turkey).

id_tips: Small, chunky quail. Rufous and brown, with a short tail. Male has a white throat and eyebrow. Female's are buff. Explodes from the grass in a covey.
habitat: Old fields, hedgerows, and open pine woods with native grasses.
wnc: Native, but greatly declined. Still found in parts of the coastal plain, sandhills, and a few piedmont and foothill farms. Scarce in the high mountains.
uses: Call is a clear bob-white. Eats seeds and insects. Coveys roost in a circle on the ground.
caution: Native and declining. Released pen-raised birds are not the same as a wild covey. Habitat, not another release, is what wild birds need.
lookalikes: Ruffed Grouse is larger, crested, and a mountain-forest bird. A meadowlark has a yellow breast and a long bill and does not explode from a covey.
wikipedia_extract: The northern bobwhite (Colinus virginianus), also known as the Virginia quail or (in its home range) bobwhite quail, is a ground-dwelling bird native to Canada, the United States, Mexico, and Cuba, with introduced populations elsewhere in the Caribbean, Europe, and Asia. It is a member of the group of species known as New World quail (Odontophoridae). They were initially placed with the Old World quail in the pheasant family (Phasianidae), but are not particularly closely related. The name "bobwhite" is an onomatopoeic derivation from its characteristic whistling call. Despite its secretive nature, the northern bobwhite is one of the most familiar quails in eastern North America, because it is frequently the only quail in its range. Habitat degradation has contributed to the northern bobwhite population in eastern North America declining by roughly 85% from 1966 to 2014. This population

id_tips: Small owl with ear tufts and yellow eyes. Two color morphs, gray and rufous, both streaked and spotted so they match bark. Often looks like a broken branch.
habitat: Wooded yards, orchards, and forests. Uses nest boxes and old woodpecker holes.
wnc: A common resident statewide wherever there are trees and cavities, including mountain towns.
uses: Call is a descending whinny and a long trill, not a scream. Eats insects, mice, and small birds.
caution: Native and protected. The whinny at dusk is this owl. Playing calls repeatedly can pull it off a nest.
lookalikes: Great Horned Owl is many times larger. Northern Saw-whet Owl is a scarce mountain winter owl with no ear tufts and a surprised expression.
wikipedia_extract: The eastern screech owl (Megascops asio) or eastern screech-owl is a stocky, short-tailed owl that is relatively common in Eastern North America, from Mexico to Canada. Mid-sized for a screech owl, the species resides in most types of woodland habitats across its range and is relatively adaptable to urban and developed areas compared to other owls. Although it often lives in close proximity to humans, the eastern screech owl frequently avoids detection due to its strictly nocturnal habits.

id_tips: A nightjar: mottled brown, huge mouth, tiny bill, and eyes that reflect light. Best known by the song. Sits lengthwise on a branch or on the ground. Hard to see.
habitat: Dry deciduous woods with an open understory, especially in the mountains.
wnc: The nightjar of cooler mountain woods. Declining. Chuck-will's-widow replaces it in the warmer lowlands.
uses: Song is a loud, repeated whip-poor-will, with the first and last syllables accented. Eats night-flying insects.
caution: Native and protected. If you hear one, you do not need a flashlight in its face. The song is the identification.
lookalikes: Chuck-will's-widow says chuck-will's-widow, a slower four-beat song, and is larger and more southern and lowland. Common Nighthawk flies over towns at dusk and calls a nasal peent.
wikipedia_extract: The eastern whip-poor-will (Antrostomus vociferus; also called "whip-o-will", "whip o' will", etc.) is a medium-sized (22–27 cm or 8.7–10.6 in) bird within the nightjar family, Caprimulgidae, from North America. The whip-poor-will is commonly heard within its range, but less often seen because of its camouflage. It is named onomatopoeically after its song.

id_tips: Largest nightjar in the East. Rufous-brown and usually invisible until it sings or flushes. The song has four beats and a lower, less clipped rhythm than a whip-poor-will.
habitat: Pine and oak woods, sandy ridges, and lower mountain slopes.
wnc: The common nightjar of the coastal plain, sandhills, and piedmont, and of warmer lower slopes in the mountains. A summer bird.
uses: Song is chuck-will's-widow, repeated. Eats large flying insects and occasionally small birds.
caution: Native and protected. Name it by the song. A glimpse on a dirt road at night is not enough to separate it from a whip-poor-will.
lookalikes: Eastern Whip-poor-will's song is faster and three-beat, and that bird is more montane. Common Nighthawk has white patches in the wing and is seen in flight at dusk.
wikipedia_extract: The chuck-will's-widow (Antrostomus carolinensis) is a nocturnal bird of the nightjar family Caprimulgidae. It is mostly found in the southeastern United States (with disjunct populations in Long Island, New York; Ontario, Canada; and Cape Cod, Massachusetts) near swamps, rocky uplands, and pine woods. It migrates to the West Indies, Central America, and northwestern South America.

id_tips: Larger than a crow, with a heavier bill, a shaggy throat, and a wedge-shaped tail. Soars and sometimes tumbles. The croak is deep.
habitat: Cliffs, high ridges, and also highway corridors where it scavenges.
wnc: A mountain bird in North Carolina, common along the Blue Ridge and Great Smokies. Rare in the piedmont and almost absent from the coastal plain.
uses: Call is a low croonk or kraa, plus many other noises. Eats carrion, insects, and whatever it can scavenge.
caution: Native and protected. In the high mountains a big black bird soaring like a hawk is often this, not a crow.
lookalikes: American Crow is smaller, fan-tailed, and says caw. If the tail is a wedge and the bird soars, it is a raven.
wikipedia_extract:
The common raven or northern raven (Corvus corax) is a large all-black passerine bird. It is the most widely distributed of all corvids, found across the Northern Hemisphere. There are 11 accepted subspecies with little variation in appearance, although recent research has demonstrated significant genetic differences among populations from various regions. It is one of the two largest corvids, alongside the thick-billed raven, and is the heaviest passerine bird; at maturity, the common raven averages 63 centimetres (25 inches) in length and 1.47 kilograms (3.2 pounds) in weight, up to 2 kg (4.4 lb) in the heaviest individuals. Although their typical lifespan is considerably shorter, common ravens can live more than 23 years in the wild. Young birds may travel in flocks but later mate for life, with each mated pair defending a territory.

id_tips: Chicken-like forest bird, mottled brown or gray, with a small crest and a fan-shaped tail barred in black. The male's black neck ruffs show in display. Explodes from the leaves with a roar of wings.
habitat: Young mountain forest, rhododendron edges, and hardwoods with dense cover.
wnc: A Southern Appalachian bird in this state. Found in the mountains, not in the piedmont or coastal plain. Numbers have fallen.
caution: Native. Hunting is regulated. Hearing the drum does not mean you will see the bird. It stands on a log and beats the air.
uses: Display is a low drum that starts slow and becomes a blur, like a distant engine. Eats buds, leaves, and fruit.
lookalikes: Northern Bobwhite is smaller, has a white or buff face pattern, and lives in grassy lowlands. Wild Turkey is far larger and bare-headed.

The ruffed grouse (Bonasa umbellus) is a medium-sized grouse occurring in forests from the Appalachian Mountains across Canada to Alaska. It is the most widely distributed game bird in North America. It is not migratory. It is the only species in the genus Bonasa. The ruffed grouse is sometimes incorrectly referred to as a "partridge", an unrelated phasianid, and occasionally confused with the grey partridge, a bird of open areas rather than woodlands.
The ruffed grouse is the state game bird of Pennsylvania, United States.

id_tips: Male is deep blue above, black on the face and throat, and white below, with a white patch on the wing. Female is olive-brown with a pale eyebrow and the same small white wing spot.
habitat: Mountain hardwoods with a rhododendron or shrub understory.
wnc: A signature breeding warbler of the Southern Appalachians. Common in summer in the mountains. Migrants pass through the rest of the state.
uses: Song is a buzzy zur-zur-zur-zreee. Eats insects. The white pocket-handkerchief on the wing marks both sexes.
caution: Native and protected. A blue-and-black warbler in a mountain cove in June is this bird.
lookalikes: Cerulean Warbler is paler blue, streaked, and a treetop bird. Indigo Bunting has no white wing spot and a conical bill.

The black-throated blue warbler (Setophaga caerulescens) is a small passerine bird of the New World warbler family. Its breeding ranges are located in the interior of deciduous and mixed coniferous forests in eastern North America. Over the cooler months, it migrates to islands in the Caribbean and Central America. It is very rarely found in western Europe, where it is considered to be a non-indigenous species. The black-throated blue warbler is sexually dimorphic; the adult male has a black face and cheeks, deep blue upperparts and white underparts, while the adult female is olive-brown above and light yellow below.

id_tips: Yellow face, olive back, black throat on the male, and two white wing bars. The female's throat is mottled rather than solid black. Often high in hemlocks and other trees.
habitat: Mountain conifers and mixed forest. Also migrants in lowland woods.
wnc: A common summer warbler of the mountains, especially where hemlock and white pine remain. Heard on the Parkway and in cove forest.
uses: Song is a buzzy zee-zee-zee-zoo-zee, or trees-trees-murmuring-trees. Eats insects.
caution: Native and protected. Hemlock loss has hurt some of its favorite habitat.
lookalikes: Hooded Warbler has a black hood all the way around a yellow face and stays lower. Blackburnian Warbler has a fiery orange throat.

id_tips: Tiny, dark brown, with a very short tail cocked straight up and faint barring on the belly. Creeps through root tangles and mossy logs like a mouse.
habitat: Breeds in high-elevation rhododendron and spruce. Winters in damp thickets at lower elevations.
wnc: Breeds in the higher mountains. In winter it is a quiet skulker in brush statewide, easier to hear than see.
uses: Song is a long, astonishing tumble of high notes. Call is a double kip-kip. Eats insects and spiders.
caution: Native and protected. It is much smaller and darker than a Carolina Wren and has only a faint eyebrow.
lookalikes: Carolina Wren is larger, rusty, and has a bold white eyebrow. House Wren is plainer and is a summer bird of brush and boxes, not a mossy spruce tangle.

The winter wren (Troglodytes hiemalis) is a very small North American bird and a member of the mainly New World wren family Troglodytidae. The species was formerly often lumped together with Eurasian wren (Troglodytes troglodytes) of Eurasia and Pacific wren (Troglodytes pacificus) of western North America under the merged name of northern wren (with the scientific name T. troglodytes having priority), until they were split in 2010.
It breeds in coniferous forests from British Columbia to the Atlantic Ocean. It migrates through and winters across southeastern Canada, the eastern half the United States and (rarely) north-eastern Mexico. Small numbers may be casual in the western United States and Canada.

habitat: Beaches, inlets, and piers. Nests on coastal islands.
wnc: A coast bird. Common along the Atlantic beaches and sounds. Not a mountain bird. Rare far inland after storms.
uses: Mostly silent. Eats fish, diving from the air. Often flies in lines just over the waves.
caution: Native and protected. Do not feed pelicans, and do not approach a hooked bird. Call a rehabilitator if one is tangled in line.
lookalikes: American White Pelican is white with black wingtips, soars inland more often, and scoops fish while swimming rather than plunge-diving. It is less common than this bird on Carolina beaches.
wikipedia_extract: The brown pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) is a bird of the pelican family, Pelecanidae, one of three species found in the Americas and one of two that feed by diving into water. It is found on the Atlantic Coast from New Jersey to the mouth of the Amazon River, and along the Pacific Coast from British Columbia to Peru, including the Galapagos Islands. The nominate subspecies in its breeding plumage has a white head with a yellowish wash on the crown. The nape and neck are dark maroon–brown. The upper sides of the neck have white lines along the base of the gular pouch, and the lower fore neck has a pale yellowish patch. The male and female are similar, but the female is slightly smaller. The nonbreeding adult has a white head and neck. The pink skin around the eyes becomes dull and gray in the nonbreeding season. habitat: Beaches, marshes, and coastal parking lots.
wnc: The common summer gull of the North Carolina coast. Scarce inland, though a few show up on reservoirs.
uses: Call is a loud ha-ha-ha. Eats fish, invertebrates, and handouts. Nests in coastal colonies.
caution: Native and protected. Feeding gulls in a parking lot creates bold birds and a mess. Don't.
lookalikes: Ring-billed Gull has a yellow bill with a black ring and no black hood. Bonaparte's Gull is smaller, with a thin black bill and white wedges in the wing.
wikipedia_extract: The laughing gull (Leucophaeus atricilla) is a medium-sized gull of North and South America. Named from its laugh-like call, it is an opportunistic omnivore and scavenger. It breeds in large colonies mostly along the Atlantic coast of North America, the Caribbean, and northern South America. Two subspecies are accepted, L. a. atricilla, which occurs from the West Indies to the Venezuelan islands, and L. a. megalopterus, which occurs from southeast Canada down to Central America. The laughing gull was long placed in the genus Larus until its present placement in Leucophaeus.

habitat: Parking lots, landfills, reservoirs, plowed fields, and the coast.
wnc: The gull you see inland. Common in winter at piedmont lakes and even some mountain reservoirs, and year-round on the coast.
uses: Calls are high yelps. Eats fish, garbage, and earthworms in fields.
caution: Native and protected. A gull at a mountain lake in winter is often this species, not a rare seabird.
lookalikes: Herring Gull is larger, with a red spot on a yellow bill and pink legs. Laughing Gull has a dark hood in summer and a dark bill.
wikipedia_extract: The ring-billed gull (Larus delawarensis) is a medium-sized gull native to North America, breeding in Canada and the northern Contiguous United States, and wintering mainly in the United States and northern Mexico. habitat: Beaches, inlets, and coastal islands.
wnc: A common warm-season tern of the North Carolina coast. Not an inland or mountain bird except as a storm stray.
uses: Call is a loud keer. Eats small fish. Nests in dense colonies on bare sand.
caution: Native and protected. Stay out of posted nesting colonies. A flushed colony can lose its eggs to heat and gulls in minutes.
lookalikes: Caspian Tern is larger, with a thicker red-orange bill and more black on the underside of the wingtips. Sandwich Tern has a black bill tipped in yellow.
wikipedia_extract: The royal tern (Thalasseus maximus) is a tern in the family Laridae. The species is endemic to the Americas, though vagrants have been identified in Europe.

id_tips: Large plain gray-brown sandpiper with a long straight bill. In flight the wings flash a bold black-and-white pattern. Legs are gray.
habitat: Salt marshes, mudflats, and beaches.
wnc: A coastal shorebird. Common on North Carolina marshes and beaches in the warmer months, and some stay through winter. Not a mountain bird.
uses: Call is a loud pill-will-willet. Eats crabs, worms, and other invertebrates.
caution: Native and protected. The wing pattern is the identification. At rest it looks almost unmarked.
lookalikes: Greater Yellowlegs has bright yellow legs and no bold wing stripe. Godwits have longer, slightly upturned bills.
wikipedia_extract: The willet (Tringa semipalmata) is a large shorebird in the family Scolopacidae. It is a relatively large and robust sandpiper and is the largest of the species called "shanks" in the genus Tringa. Its closest relative is the lesser yellowlegs, a much smaller bird with a very different appearance apart from the fine, clear, and dense pattern of the neck, which both species show in breeding plumage. It breeds in North America and the West Indies and winters in southern North America, Central America, the West Indies and South America.

id_tips: Gray breast, white throat, and yellow spots in front of the eyes. Head stripes are either bright white or tan. Scratches in leaves under feeders.
habitat: Thickets, wooded edges, and backyard brush in the cooler months.
wnc: One of the most common winter birds in the state, from the coast into mountain towns. Breeds far to the north, not in North Carolina.
uses: Song is Old Sam Peabody, Peabody, Peabody, heard even in winter. Eats seeds and scratches with both feet.
caution: Native and protected. A sparrow with a white throat and yellow lores at a winter feeder is this bird.
lookalikes: White-crowned Sparrow has a pink or yellow bill, bold black-and-white crown stripes, and no yellow lores or bright white throat patch. It is much less common here.
wikipedia_extract: The white-throated sparrow (Zonotrichia albicollis) is a passerine bird of the New World sparrow family Passerellidae. It breeds in northern North America and winters in the southern United States.

id_tips: Large duck with a bare red warty face and a slight crest. Wild-type birds are black with white wing patches. Park birds are often white or piebald. The tail is fairly long.
habitat: Town ponds and parks. Not a migrant of wild marshes.
wnc: Introduced. Domestic and feral birds occur at parks and neighborhoods in parts of North Carolina. They are not a native wild duck and do not belong on a list of wild migrants.
uses: Quiet hisses and puffing rather than a mallard quack. Eats whatever people throw, plus pond plants and insects.
caution: Introduced and feral. Do not release pet ducks. Do not count a red-faced park duck as a rare wild species. Bread is bad for them and for the water.
lookalikes: Mallards have a normal feathered face. A male Wood Duck is brightly patterned and crested but has no red warts.
wikipedia_extract: The Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata) is a species of duck native to the Americas, from the Lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas and Mexico south to Argentina and Uruguay. The species has been domesticated, and feral Muscovy ducks can be found locally in New Zealand, Australia, the United States, and in Central and Eastern Europe.

id_tips: Small, stocky white heron with a short yellow bill and dark legs. In breeding season the crown, breast, and back are washed buff-orange. Often walks in pastures among cows.
habitat: Pastures, fields, and wet meadows. Roosts and nests in colonies with other herons.
wnc: Arrived in the Americas on its own in the 1900s and is now a regular breeding bird in North Carolina, especially the coastal plain and piedmont. Treat it as native, not as an introduced invasive. Less common in the high mountains.
uses: Mostly quiet. Eats insects stirred up by livestock and mowers, not mostly fish.
caution: Native and protected. It is not a farm pest to be removed. The cattle are a field mark.
lookalikes: Great Egret is much taller, with a longer yellow bill and black legs. Snowy Egret has a black bill and yellow feet. A Cattle Egret looks neckless by comparison.
wikipedia_extract:
The cattle egrets (formerly genus Bubulcus) are a cosmopolitan clade of herons (family Ardeidae) in the genus Ardea found in the tropics, subtropics, warm temperate, and increasingly in cooler temperate zones. As currently treated, the clade contains two species, the western cattle egret and the eastern cattle egret, although some authorities (particularly in the past) regarded them as a single species. Despite the similarities in plumage to the egrets of the genus Egretta, they have recently been found to be genetically embedded within the genus Ardea, and are now included there. Originally native to parts of Asia, Africa, and southernmost Europe, the two species have undergone rapid expansion in their distribution and have successfully colonised much of the rest of the world in the last century.
They are white birds adorned with buff plumes in the breeding season. They nest in colonies

id_tips: The whole head is crimson. The body is black and white in big blocks: white underparts, white wing patches, and a black back. No zebra barring.
habitat: Open groves, dead timber, beaver ponds, and savannas.
wnc: Native but local. More often in the coastal plain and piedmont than in closed mountain forest. Needs standing dead trees.
uses: Call is a harsh queer. Eats insects, acorns, and fruit, and catches insects in flight. Stores food in cracks.
caution: Native and declining. Removing every dead tree removes this bird. It is not the same as the common Red-bellied Woodpecker.
lookalikes: Red-bellied Woodpecker has a pale face, a red crown and nape only, and a barred back. If the entire head is red and the wings are big white patches, it is this bird.
wikipedia_extract:
The red-headed woodpecker (Melanerpes erythrocephalus) is a mid-sized woodpecker found in temperate North America. Its breeding habitat is open country across southern Canada and the east-central United States. It is rated as least concern on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN)'s Red List of Endangered species, having been down-listed from near threatened in 2018.
The red-headed woodpecker should not be confused with the red-bellied woodpecker, which is similar in size but has a vibrant orange-red crown and nape; the red-bellied woodpecker is named for the pale reddish blush of its lower belly and has a distinctly patterned black and white back rather than the solid black one of the red-headed woodpecker.

id_tips: Constantly fans the tail. Male is black with bright orange patches on the sides, wings, and tail. Female and young males are gray-olive with yellow where the male is orange.
habitat: Young deciduous woods and edges.
wnc: A common summer warbler statewide, especially in second-growth and mountain coves.
uses: Song is a series of high, sneezing notes. Eats insects, often by fly-catching. The flashing tail startles prey.
caution: Native and protected. The name redstart is shared with an unrelated European bird. This is the North American warbler.
lookalikes: Nothing else here flashes orange or yellow tail patches like this. A Blackburnian Warbler has an orange throat but does not fan orange tail sides.
wikipedia_extract: The American redstart (Setophaga ruticilla) is a New World warbler. It is only distantly related to the Old World (common) redstart, with both belonging to the order Passeriformes.
